title: Gravitational wave astronomy
one_line_summary: Turns the gravitational-wave theory of Chapter 9 into observational practice: a tour of the source classes (compact binaries, spinning neutron stars, bursts, stochastic backgrounds) with solar-mass-normalised scaling laws, a discrete-sample introduction to how interferometer data are turned into detections (detector tensor and antenna patterns, noise spectra, matched filtering, false-alarm statistics, coincidence and time slides, null streams, pulsar and stochastic searches), and a narrative of the first LIGO-Virgo events (GW150914, GW170814, GW170817, GW190425, GW190521, GW190814) and what each taught.
role_in_book: New in the third edition, this chapter sits between the black-hole chapter (11) and cosmology (13) and is the payoff of Chapter 9: the chirp mass, time-to-merger, polarization-versus-inclination and standard-siren results derived there are now used on real data, and the Kerr ringdown and intermediate-mass black holes of Chapter 11 reappear as observed phenomena. It is the book's only sustained treatment of signal analysis and statistics, and it ends by pointing to Chapter 13 through the Hubble-Lemaitre constant measured with GW170817 and through the cosmological gravitational-wave background. Almost no new geometry is introduced; the tensor language is used once, elegantly, for the detector response.

assumed_background.topic: Transverse-traceless gauge, plus and cross polarizations, and the effect of a wave on free test masses
Quadrupole radiation from a rotating body and from a circular binary, including the inclination dependence of the two polarizations (Eqs. 9.84-9.86, 9.98-9.100)
Chirp mass, orbital decay, time to merger and orbital phase remaining (Eqs. 9.156-9.159) and detector-frame redshifted masses (Eq. 9.163)
Standard-siren distance measurement from binary chirps
Interferometric detectors, arm-length strain, LISA and the ground-based network
Kerr black holes, quasi-normal modes, supermassive and intermediate-mass black holes
Outer product of vectors and full contraction of tensors
Geometrized units with G = c = 1 and conversion of masses to seconds (1 solar mass is about 4.9 microseconds)
Gaussian probability distributions, mean, variance, standard deviation, central limit theorem
Discrete Fourier transforms, convolution and the idea of a power spectrum
Inverse of a 2x2 matrix and determinants
Basic stellar astrophysics: supernovae, pulsars, X-ray binaries, gamma-ray bursts, redshift and the Hubble law
Doppler shift and the diffraction limit of an aperture
Integration by parts and asymptotic bounds on integrals

learning_objectives: Reader can contrast gravitational and electromagnetic radiation as information carriers (what emits them, typical frequencies, coherence over the source, absorption, focusing, localization) and explain why they are complementary.

Reader can estimate the gravitational-wave frequency at which a compact binary effectively merges, the remaining time to merger from a given frequency, and the ringdown frequency of the remnant, all scaled to solar masses.

Reader can explain the formation puzzles for merging black-hole binaries (natal kicks, common envelopes, low metallicity, dynamical and triple channels) and how spin alignment could discriminate among them.
Reader can estimate the strain from a slightly non-axisymmetric spinning neutron star and explain why long coherent integration and the spin-down limit matter for continuous-wave searches.
Reader can write the detector response as the double contraction of a detector tensor with the wave tensor and decompose it into antenna pattern functions F+ and Fx.
Reader can read an amplitude spectral density plot and attribute its low-, mid- and high-frequency walls to seismic/Newtonian, thermal and shot noise, and distinguish Gaussian noise from glitches.
Reader can derive, for white noise, the matched-filter threshold A_min = sigma/||w|| and show that it improves on simple threshold crossing by roughly the square root of the number of signal cycles.
Reader can compute Gaussian false-alarm probabilities with the tail bound, include the trials factor from many samples and templates, and justify signal-to-noise thresholds near 8.
Reader can explain coincidence analysis, time slides, and why a network of three or more detectors enables coherent analysis, null streams, glitch vetoes, direction finding and calibration checks.

Reader can reconstruct the two polarizations from two detectors with known sky position and infer the orbital inclination from the amplitude ratio, and explain the distance-inclination degeneracy for nearly face-on systems.

Reader can explain why Doppler modulation from Earth's motion makes optimal all-sky pulsar searches computationally impossible, and estimate the resulting angular resolution and number of sky patches.
Reader can derive the cross-correlation signal-to-noise ratio for a stochastic background and explain its slow fourth-root growth in amplitude.

Reader can summarize what GW150914, GW170814, GW170817, GW190425, GW190521 and GW190814 each established (black-hole binaries exist, tensor polarization, multimessenger kilonova and r-process, standard-siren H0, mass-gap objects, higher multipoles).
Reader can explain how a standard-siren distance plus a host-galaxy redshift yields the Hubble-Lemaitre constant, and why inclination uncertainty dominates the error.

teaching_approach.summary: An observational survey chapter written by a practitioner of gravitational-wave data analysis. Instead of geometry it teaches order-of-magnitude scaling, statistical reasoning and detection strategy. Every data-analysis idea is built from the simplest discrete model (sampled white Gaussian noise plus a known template) so that results like the square-root-of-N gain, the Gaussian false-alarm tail and the N^(1/4) stochastic scaling can be derived in a few lines, then corrected qualitatively for real coloured noise, glitches and huge parameter spaces. The detection stories at the end are used as case studies for the analysis concepts introduced earlier (glitch removal, antenna-pattern nulls, inclination errors, higher harmonics).
narrative_arc: Open with the Figure 12.1 time series of GW150914 in both LIGO detectors as proof that observational gravitational-wave astronomy exists.

Contrast gravitational and electromagnetic radiation (coherent global emission versus microscopic emission; low versus high frequencies; unfocusable versus imaging) to motivate multimessenger astronomy and to justify why theory of sources had to precede detection.

Survey source classes: binaries (merger frequency, time to merger, LISA-to-ground handoff, formation channels, ringdown, EMRIs), spinning neutron stars (strain estimate, spin-down limits), unmodelled bursts (supernovae, cosmic strings), stochastic backgrounds (astrophysical and cosmological, Omega_gw), and unknown sources.
Pose the question 'what counts as a detection?' and set up the detector response with a detector tensor, antenna patterns and network patterns.
Describe detector noise: amplitude spectral density, Gaussianity from the central limit theorem, shot/thermal/seismic walls, lines, Newtonian noise, glitches.
Build matched filtering from a toy model of sampled data, compare its threshold with naive threshold crossing, and extract the square-root-of-cycles gain.

Move from detection to measurement: template banks, intrinsic versus extrinsic parameters, Bayesian posteriors, polarization reconstruction with two detectors and inclination from the polarization ratio.
Quantify significance with Gaussian tail probabilities, real sample counts and trials factors; then confront glitches with coincidence and time slides.
Use a counting argument (two polarizations, N detectors) to motivate coherent analysis and derive the three-detector null stream and its uses.
Apply the principles class by class: Doppler-modulated pulsar searches and their impossible computing cost, cross-correlation searches for backgrounds, minimal-assumption burst searches.
Tell the story of the first detections as case studies, closing with catalogs, rising detection rates and the expanding network.
signature_moves: Normalises every astrophysical formula to one solar mass and a benchmark frequency so readers can plug in real systems instantly (Eqs. 12.1-12.4).
Teaches signal processing with discrete samples and Kronecker deltas instead of continuous power spectral densities, deferring the frequency domain to an exercise.
Derives a scaling law from the simplest possible case (a pure sinusoid, co-located aligned detectors) and then argues it is robust.
Converts abstract probabilities into countable events using actual sampling rates and run lengths (140,000 five-sigma fluctuations per year).
Uses counting arguments (unknown functions versus data streams) to reveal structure such as the null stream before doing any algebra.
Estimates computing cost in floating-point operations to show that an optimal search is out of reach, making the case for suboptimal methods quantitatively.
Treats the detection narratives as worked illustrations of earlier analysis ideas (glitch in GW170817, Virgo's antenna-pattern null, higher multipoles in GW190521).
Keeps flagging dates ('mid-2021') and open problems, presenting the field as live rather than finished.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Announces the first direct detection and uses the two-detector strain traces as the chapter's emblem. Sets up a systematic comparison of gravitational with electromagnetic waves: gravitational waves come from bulk mass-energy motions and encode global properties at nHz-kHz frequencies, pass through matter but cannot be focused, so detectors are nearly omnidirectional and only energetic relativistic sources are seen; light comes from microscopic charges at far higher frequencies, is absorbed and scattered but can be imaged. Both travel at c, are transverse, and can be lensed. The complementarity motivates multimessenger astronomy, while the differences warn against expecting counterparts. Explains that source theory was needed both to justify the investment and because predicted waveforms raise effective sensitivity.
concepts: complementarity of gravitational and electromagnetic observations
key_moves: The sign flip and time shift between Hanford and Livingston traces encode detector geometry and sky position.
Emission from coherent bulk motion versus incoherent microscopic charges explains the frequency and information contrast.
Weak coupling to matter is both a virtue (transparency) and a limitation (no focusing, only high-flux sources).
Waveform prediction is part of detector sensitivity, which is why theory was essential before detection.

sections.title: Astrophysical sources of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Groups sources into binaries, spinning neutron stars, bursts and the Big Bang. For binaries, notes that only mass ratio, eccentricity and separation matter once total mass sets the scale; slowly evolving binaries fill the LISA and pulsar-timing bands (white-dwarf confusion noise, supermassive black-hole background), whereas ground-based detectors see mergers. Rearranges the Chapter 9 phase-to-merger relation into a merger-frequency estimate (half an orbit left), checks it against GW150914 and binary neutron stars, derives the upper mass limit set by LIGO's 20 Hz floor, and rescales the time-to-merger formula to show that a 30 solar-mass chirp-mass system seen by LISA at 30 mHz merges in the ground band within a year. Discusses why merging compact binaries are hard to form (supernova kicks, common envelopes) and the low-metallicity, cluster, triple and primordial channels, the X-ray binary and binary-pulsar evidence, the short gamma-ray burst connection, LISA supermassive mergers, ringdown frequencies and EMRIs.
concepts: short gamma-ray bursts from neutron star mergers
key_moves: Invert psi = (1/32)(M omega)^(-5/3) for f_gw = omega/pi and set psi = pi to get f_final = 4.0 kHz (1 solar mass / chirp mass).
Check: GW150914 predicts 130 Hz against an observed peak near 250 Hz, a factor of two accepted for such a crude estimate.
A 20 Hz low-frequency cutoff means chirp masses above about 200 solar masses merge below the ground-based band.
Rescaled time-to-merger: 2.9 s at 100 Hz for one solar mass, steeply dependent on mass (-5/3) and frequency (-8/3).
Ringdown at omega about 0.5/M gives 16 kHz per solar mass, 230 Hz for GW150914's remnant.
Spin alignment as a fossil record of isolated-binary versus dynamical formation.

sections.title: Spinning neutron stars, bursts, stochastic backgrounds and unexpected sources (within 12.2)
sections.summary: Continuous-wave sources: a rotating neutron star with fractional asymmetry epsilon radiates h ~ 2 epsilon Omega^2 I / r, about 1e-26 for a millisecond-scale pulsar at 1 kpc with epsilon = 1e-6; reaching such amplitudes needs about 1e8 coherent cycles. Searches have found nothing; limits reach epsilon ~ 1e-7, and for the Crab the gravitational share of spin-down energy loss is tiny. Bursts: core-collapse supernovae cannot be predicted in detail, so they are sought as excess power, ideally in coincidence with neutrinos; cosmic strings are a speculative burst source. Stochastic backgrounds: random superpositions measured by cross-correlating detectors, characterised by mean square amplitude and Omega_gw; the LIGO pair correlates below about 100 Hz; Figure 12.2 shows the predicted binary black hole background and LIGO sensitivity; a cosmological background would probe the earliest Universe but is probably out of reach except via CMB polarization. Ends by hoping for entirely unanticipated sources, possibly linked to dark matter.
concepts: continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars
energy density parameter of gravitational waves
key_moves: Amplitude estimate from the Chapter 9 rotating-quadrupole formula with realistic moment of inertia.
Narrowband integration concentrates signal power into one frequency bin while noise spreads, so sensitivity grows as the square root of observing time.
Spin-down sets an energy-based upper bound; amplitude limits below it translate quadratically into energy fractions.
Correlation between two sites persists for wavelengths longer than the separation, fixing the usable band.
The CMB is the electromagnetic analogue of a cosmological gravitational background, but gravity decoupled essentially at the beginning.

sections.title: Finding weak signals in noise: what is a detection?
sections.summary: Frames every detection as a probabilistic statement with a false-alarm estimate. Sets up two frames: detector-based spherical coordinates and a sky-plane basis attached to the wave. Builds plus and cross basis tensors, writes the wave as a TT tensor, defines the detector tensor L(e_x e_x - e_y e_y), and obtains the arm-length difference as a double contraction; dividing by L gives the response F+ h+ + Fx hx with geometry-only antenna functions. Plots the antenna power pattern for one interferometer and the LIGO-Virgo network. Then describes intrinsic noise via the amplitude spectral density: mostly Gaussian by the central limit theorem, with shot noise at high frequency, thermal noise in the bucket, seismic noise at low frequency, narrow suspension and mains lines, design trade-offs (laser power, cryogenics), Newtonian noise that motivates underground and space detectors, and non-Gaussian glitches that limit burst searches.
concepts: amplitude spectral density of detector noise
key_moves: Keep the wave's sky-plane basis independent of any detector so the same wave can be projected onto many detectors.
Response = d : h, a coordinate-free double contraction (the tensor-as-machine idea applied to hardware).
Separate geometry (F+, Fx depending on theta, phi) from waveform (h+, hx).
Network power pattern is the sum of individual patterns for identical detectors; holes remain.
Shot noise rises with frequency because fewer photons arrive per shorter sample interval.

sections.title: Matched filtering, template banks and parameter extraction (within 12.3)
sections.summary: GW170817 never exceeded 1e-22 yet had the highest significance, because its waveform was known. With sampled data x_j = n_j + A w_(j-D) in white Gaussian noise, naive threshold crossing requires A above sigma / w_max, whereas correlating with the template gives a Gaussian statistic whose mean peaks at the arrival index with value A||w||^2 and whose standard deviation is sigma||w||, so the threshold becomes sigma/||w||. For a sinusoid this is lower by sqrt(N/2), better read as the square root of the number of cycles because resampling changes sigma and N together; range grows as that factor and volume as its cube. Realistic searches use banks of thousands of post-Newtonian plus numerical-relativity templates, computed with FFTs in the frequency domain, currently for quasi-circular orbits; LISA adds orbital modulation and the EMRI template problem. The best-matching template gives intrinsic parameters (chirp mass best, then total mass, component masses and spins) with Bayesian posteriors; extrinsic parameters need a network. Two detectors with a known sky position invert a 2x2 matrix to recover h+ and hx; rotating the sky basis until they are in quadrature gives the inclination from their amplitude ratio, which is poorly constrained near face-on, feeding a distance-inclination degeneracy that higher harmonics can break.
key_moves: Model data as noise plus a shifted, scaled template; compute mean and variance of the correlation.
Replace the template's peak value by its norm: the norm integrates over the signal's duration.
Sinusoid example: squared norm is B^2 N/2 because the cos(2 omega t) term averages out.
Resampling argument shows the gain counts cycles, not samples.
Matrix inversion of the two-detector response (Eqs. 12.23-12.25).
Quadrature criterion fixes the sky-basis rotation, giving |h+|/|hx| = (1 + cos^2 iota)/(2 cos iota).

sections.title: What is a detection? Significance, coincidence and time slides (within 12.3)
sections.summary: Uses the two-sided Gaussian tail probability and its bounds to show that a 5 sigma fluctuation, rare per sample, occurs about 140,000 times in a year of 8 kHz data; per independent filter sample (about 5 ms) the threshold must rise to about 6.5 for one false alarm every two years, and with 1e4 independent templates to about 8. Glitches make single-detector thresholds unreliable, so LIGO works in coincidence mode with a light-travel-time window; residual coincident glitches are measured by time slides that destroy true coincidences but preserve the glitch rate. Mentions that a Bayesian likelihood-ratio approach would be deeper than this frequentist treatment.
key_moves: Upper tail bound phi(a)/a becomes accurate for large a (proved in Exercise 12.5).
Count samples in a year to turn tiny probabilities into expected false alarms.
Each template is an independent trial, multiplying the false-alarm rate.
Shifting one detector's data by more than the coincidence window yields a pure-background sample.

sections.title: Coherent detection by a network and the null stream (within 12.3)
sections.summary: Coincidence uses only arrival times and amplitudes; with three or more detectors one can combine outputs before thresholding. Counting: a wave is two functions of time, so two non-aligned detectors can solve for them given the direction, three can find the direction with redundancy, and redundancy produces signal-free combinations. For three detectors, eliminating h+ and hx gives D12 delta3 + D23 delta1 + D31 delta2 = 0, where D_ab are 2x2 determinants of antenna factors; applied to the noisy outputs this null stream contains only noise and glitches. Uses: veto coincident glitches (bringing thresholds down to the Gaussian floor), measure and subtract a glitch overlapping a signal, find the sky direction as the one that nulls the signal, and test calibration consistency. Credits the aperture-synthesis analogy.
key_moves: Count unknown waveforms against data streams to predict the number of null streams (N - 2).
Substitute the two-detector solution into the third response to eliminate the signal.
A wrong assumed direction leaves signal in the null stream, so minimizing null power locates the source.
The null stream vanishes only if relative calibrations are right.

sections.title: Searching for pulsars, stochastic backgrounds and unmodelled bursts (within 12.3)
sections.summary: Pulsars: Earth's rotation and orbit Doppler-modulate a continuous signal; equating the accumulated frequency shift to the frequency resolution gives a coherent time of about 70 minutes (rotation) or a few hours (orbit) at 1 kHz, far shorter than the months needed. Demodulation depends on direction, so the orbit acts as a synthesized aperture with resolution about lambda/2R, some 0.4 arcsec at 1 kHz, requiring about 1e12 sky patches, multiplied by thousands to millions of spin-down values: optimal all-sky searches exceed world computing power (Exercise 12.9), so searches are suboptimal; targeted searches of known pulsars and Sco X-1 are easier. Stochastic: for co-located aligned detectors the correlation has mean N|h|^2 and standard deviation sqrt(N) sigma1 sigma2, so power SNR grows as N^(1/2) and amplitude SNR as N^(1/4); a background 1e4 below noise would need 1e16 samples, but a year at an effective 100 Hz reaches about 100 times below noise. LISA uses its Sagnac null stream to measure its own noise; pulsar timing correlates pulsars. Bursts: require strong signals, neutrino coincidence for supernovae, cosmic-string spectral templates, and sine-Gaussian banks; GW150914 was first flagged by such a burst search.
concepts: angular resolution by orbital aperture synthesis
computational cost of all-sky continuous-wave searches
key_moves: Velocity change Omega^2 R T gives frequency drift f Omega^2 R T / c; equate to resolution 2/T.
Diffraction-limit resolution lambda/(2R) with R the orbital radius.
Number of patches 4 pi / (Delta theta)^2 times number of spin-down bins shows the combinatorial explosion.
Correlation of two streams: signal term N|h|^2, dominant variance N sigma1^2 sigma2^2.
Effective sample rate for correlation is set by the band where the detectors are correlated (about 100 Hz).

Doppler-modulated pulsar signals are too intricate to be mimicked by instrumental artefacts, so single-detector searches with Gaussian false-alarm statistics are acceptable, with other detectors used for follow-up.

sections.title: The first LIGO and Virgo detections
sections.summary: Opens by recalling what was expected before 2015: at design sensitivity Advanced LIGO should see roughly one event a year, most likely a binary neutron star near 100 Mpc, and with O1 running two to three times below design the first detection seemed years off. Then narrates GW150914: detected during an engineering run, a century after the field equations, first spotted by collaboration members in Hanover, recognisable as a binary black hole because its chirp was too fast and too strong for neutron stars; its parameters, graviton-mass bound, why the objects are called black holes, the unexpected size of its component masses and support for low-metallicity formation; O1's two further events. O2 added four LIGO-only black-hole events (GW170729 the farthest at 2.8 Gpc). GW170814 was the first three-detector event, shrinking the sky area and testing tensor versus pure scalar or vector polarization. GW170817 is treated in depth: 100 s in band, a gamma-ray burst 1.7 s after merger, a Livingston glitch removed by hand, Virgo's weak response used as directional information, 31 square degrees and 40 Mpc, the kilonova found in NGC4993 within 11 hours, masses, spin assumptions, Love-number limits, an off-axis jet, the first standard-siren H0 and its later radio-improved value, r-process element production, and how lucky its closeness was.
concepts: r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers
key_moves: Identification of a binary black hole from chirp rate and amplitude alone.
Dispersion from a graviton mass accumulates over the propagation distance, so distant sources give strong bounds.
An antenna-pattern null in one detector still carries directional information.
H0 = recession velocity / standard-siren distance; inclination is the main error source.
Tidal effects scale as 1/r^3 and so appear only in the last orbits.

sections.title: Further observations and catalogs (within 12.4)
sections.summary: GW190425: likely binary neutron star with total mass about 3.4 solar masses, seen significantly only by Livingston, poorly localized, no counterpart. GW190521: about 150 solar masses total, only four cycles (two orbits) in band, formed an intermediate-mass black hole; its 85 solar-mass primary is heavier than stellar collapse is expected to produce (the book does not name the pair-instability gap), suggesting an earlier merger; a possible AGN flare counterpart; and higher multipoles that moved the inferred distance from 4.1 to 5.3 Gpc. GW190814: 23 plus 2.6 solar masses, a mass-gap companion, 9:1 mass ratio whose higher harmonics sharpened the inclination and enabled a statistical H0 without a host. Catalogs GWTC-1 and GWTC-2, the rising detection rate driven by cubic volume scaling and lower thresholds, the trade-off between false positives and missed events, and the prospect of a five-detector network.
key_moves: Higher multipoles have different angular patterns, so they break the distance-inclination degeneracy.
Halving amplitude noise doubles range and multiplies searched volume by eight.
A false-alarm threshold of two per year accepts about one spurious event in 39 in exchange for not discarding real ones.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Points to live web resources (event pages, LIGO companion papers, open data and audio, Einstein@Home, Gravity Spy, LISA site) and to books and reviews on detectors, the sociology of the first detection, neutron-star physics, kilonovae, post-Newtonian theory, tests of general relativity with LISA and ground detectors, and statistical data analysis.
concepts: citizen science in gravitational wave analysis
key_moves: Directs the reader to participate (volunteer computing, glitch classification) rather than only read.

concepts.name: gravitational wave astronomy
concepts.definition: The study of astrophysical and cosmological systems through the gravitational radiation they emit, using detectors that measure the tidal strain of passing waves (ground interferometers, space interferometers such as LISA, pulsar timing arrays).
concepts.how_introduced: Opened with the Figure 12.1 strain traces of GW150914 as the moment the field became observational, then justified as a genuinely new window by comparing it point by point with electromagnetic astronomy.

concepts.name: complementarity of gravitational and electromagnetic observations
concepts.definition: Gravitational waves are generated coherently by bulk motions of mass-energy, carry global source properties at low frequencies (nHz to kHz), penetrate matter and cannot be focused; electromagnetic waves come from microscopic charges, carry local physical information at high frequencies, are absorbed and scattered but can be imaged. Each reveals what the other hides.
concepts.how_introduced: Laid out as a structured contrast (source of emission, frequency range, interaction with matter, focusing and localization, source requirements) followed by shared properties (speed c, transverse polarization, lensing).
concepts.notes: Also used to explain why EM observations cannot reliably predict the gravitational-wave source population.

concepts.name: multimessenger astronomy
concepts.definition: Coordinated observation of the same astrophysical event through different carriers (gravitational waves, photons across the spectrum, neutrinos, cosmic rays) so that each channel constrains what the others cannot.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the complementarity argument in the overview and realized spectacularly by GW170817 with its gamma-ray burst and kilonova; supernova searches with neutrino coincidence are a second example.
prerequisites: complementarity of gravitational and electromagnetic observations

concepts.name: gravitational lensing of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Deflection and magnification of gravitational waves by intervening masses, exactly as for light; apart from lensing, a freely propagating gravitational wave's amplitude is not brightened or dimmed along its path.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed briefly among the similarities between the two kinds of radiation.

concepts.name: chirp mass
concepts.definition: The mass combination (m1 m2)^(3/5)/(m1 + m2)^(1/5) that alone controls the leading-order (quadrupole, Newtonian-orbit) frequency evolution of an inspiralling binary; it is therefore the best-measured binary parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 9 as the normalizing mass in the merger-frequency and time-to-merger scalings, then used to explain parameter-estimation hierarchies (chirp mass to better than 1 percent, other masses worse) and in Exercise 12.11.
concepts.notes: The text quotes 30.8 solar masses for GW150914 while Table 12.1 gives 28; the table lists redshift-corrected source-frame values, and the larger number is presumably closer to the detector-frame value (the book does not say which frame it used).

concepts.name: mass ratio of a binary
concepts.definition: The ratio of the smaller to the larger component mass, taken here in the range 0 < m2/m1 <= 0.5 by the stated convention, which together with eccentricity and semi-major axis (in units of total mass) specifies a point-mass binary.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to argue that binaries are the simplest and most reliably modelled radiating systems in astronomy because so few parameters are needed.
concepts.notes: The stated upper bound 0.5 is odd: equal masses give 1, and the chapter later discusses near-equal-mass systems; the usual convention is 0 < q <= 1. The same symbol epsilon is reused for neutron-star asymmetry and in Exercise 12.7.

concepts.name: merger frequency estimate
concepts.definition: An order-of-magnitude estimate of the highest gravitational-wave frequency a point-mass inspiral reaches, obtained from the leading-order phase-to-merger relation by evaluating the frequency when half an orbit (orbital phase pi) remains: f_final is about 4.0 kHz times (one solar mass divided by the chirp mass).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the formal divergence of frequency for point particles; checked against GW150914 (130 Hz predicted, about 250 Hz observed) and binary neutron stars (a few kHz predicted, but tidal disruption near 1 kHz); used to derive the upper mass limit of ground-based detectors.

concepts.name: orbital phase remaining before merger
concepts.definition: The orbital phase (in radians) a Newtonian inspiral still has to accumulate before the formal coalescence; at leading order psi = (1/32)(M omega)^(-5/3) with M the chirp mass and omega the orbital angular frequency.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from Eq. 9.159 and inverted to express frequency as a function of phase left.

concepts.name: time to merger
concepts.definition: The remaining time until coalescence of a quasi-circular binary emitting at a given gravitational-wave frequency, at leading order proportional to chirp mass to the -5/3 power and frequency to the -8/3 power; 2.9 s for a one-solar-mass chirp mass at 100 Hz.
concepts.how_introduced: Rescaled from Eq. 9.158 to quantify how long a LISA-band binary takes to reach the ground band and, in exercises, how long signals stay in band.

concepts.name: multiband gravitational wave astronomy
concepts.definition: Observing the same binary at different evolutionary stages in different detector bands, e.g. a stellar-mass black-hole binary seen by LISA at tens of mHz that merges in the ground-based band months later, allowing advance prediction of merger time and sky position.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented via Sesana's suggestion and a quick time-to-merger calculation for a 30 solar-mass chirp mass at 30 mHz giving nine to ten months.

concepts.name: confusion noise
concepts.definition: An effective noise created when so many overlapping signals share a frequency band that they cannot be individually resolved; for LISA the Galactic white-dwarf binaries below about 1 mHz exceed instrumental noise, and for pulsar timing unresolved supermassive black-hole binaries form a background.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned while explaining which binaries are non-evolving in the low-frequency bands.

concepts.name: natal kick
concepts.definition: The recoil velocity a neutron star or black hole acquires at birth from an asymmetric supernova explosion; it can unbind a binary or, if directed against the orbital motion, leave an eccentric orbit with a closer periastron.
concepts.how_introduced: Part of the explanation of why compact binaries that merge within a Hubble time are rare: the system must survive two such kicks.

concepts.name: common envelope evolution
concepts.definition: A binary evolution phase in which an expanding giant engulfs its compact companion so that gas drag shrinks the orbit; if drag is too strong the companion spirals into the core (forming a Thorne-Zytkow object) instead of leaving a close compact binary.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why many astronomers doubted before 2015 that binary black holes could form, and why low metallicity (smaller giants, weaker drag) offers a loophole.

concepts.name: binary black hole formation channels
concepts.definition: Proposed routes to merging black-hole binaries: isolated evolution of low-metallicity massive binaries, dynamical capture in globular or nuclear clusters, secular evolution in hierarchical triples, and (speculatively) primordial black holes forming part of dark matter. Isolated binaries should have spins roughly aligned with the orbit; dynamical captures should have random spin orientations.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed after the common-envelope problem, with spin alignment proposed as the observational discriminator; revisited when GW150914's high masses favoured low metallicity and GW190521's 85 solar-mass primary suggested hierarchical mergers.

concepts.name: X-ray binary
concepts.definition: A close binary in which a neutron star or black hole accretes gas stripped from a normal or giant companion through a disk whose frictional heating makes it a bright X-ray source; evidence that systems can survive the first supernova.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked as astronomical evidence along the formation path of compact binaries; historical note on rocket discovery and Giacconi's Nobel Prize.
concepts.notes: Before 2015 the heaviest known stellar black holes, about 20 solar masses, were in X-ray binaries.

concepts.name: short gamma-ray bursts from neutron star mergers
concepts.definition: Brief bursts of gamma rays (the short-duration population) produced by narrow relativistic jets launched in binary neutron star (or neutron star-black hole) mergers, accompanied by a kilonova; confirmed by the GW170817/GRB170817A association.
concepts.how_introduced: History from military satellites in the 1960s through the short/long classification and the 1989 merger proposal, leading to the GW170817 confirmation.

concepts.name: kilonova
concepts.definition: An optical/infrared transient lasting days, powered by radioactive decay of heavy neutron-rich nuclei synthesized in material ejected during a neutron star merger.
concepts.how_introduced: Predicted counterpart of short bursts; observed after GW170817 by six teams within about 11 hours, then followed until it faded.
prerequisites: r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers

concepts.name: ringdown
concepts.definition: The exponentially damped oscillation with which a newly formed, distorted black hole sheds its deformations and settles to a Kerr black hole; its frequencies and damping times depend only on the final mass and spin, so they fingerprint a black hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Estimated with omega about 0.5/M, giving 16 kHz per solar mass and about 230 Hz for the GW150914 remnant, close to the observed peak frequency; later cited as the direct test of a black-hole remnant not yet claimed by LIGO-Virgo.
concepts.notes: The estimate uses f = omega/2 pi, whereas the chirp formulas use f_gw = omega/pi with omega the orbital frequency; learners may confuse the two.

concepts.name: extreme mass-ratio inspiral
concepts.definition: The slow inspiral of a stellar-mass compact object (about 10-50 solar masses) into a supermassive black hole (about a million solar masses) after capture from the surrounding cluster, radiating in the LISA band for 1e5-1e6 orbits and mapping the strong-field spacetime of the large hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as a capture-then-circularisation process, with the promise of precision strong-field tests and the theoretical challenge of building templates faithful over so many orbits.

concepts.name: continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars
concepts.definition: Nearly monochromatic, long-lived gravitational radiation from a rotating neutron star that is not symmetric about its spin axis (crustal or core deformations, r-modes, accretion-driven asymmetries), at twice the spin frequency for a rigid deformation.
concepts.how_introduced: Pulsars spin in the ground-based band; the amplitude is estimated from the rotating-quadrupole formula; discussion of search sensitivity, spin-down limits and non-detections.

concepts.name: neutron star ellipticity
concepts.definition: A dimensionless measure of how far a neutron star's mass distribution departs from axisymmetry about its rotation axis, roughly the fractional difference of equatorial moments of inertia; gravitational-wave strain is proportional to it.
concepts.how_introduced: Enters the strain estimate with the illustrative value 1e-6; observational upper limits of about 1e-7 for some pulsars and a few times 1e-5 for the Crab show neutron stars are remarkably axisymmetric.

concepts.name: spin-down limit
concepts.definition: The maximum gravitational-wave amplitude a pulsar could emit if all its observed rotational energy loss went into gravitational waves; measured upper limits below this bound constrain the fraction of spin-down that is gravitational, which scales as the square of the amplitude ratio.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained for the Crab pulsar, whose amplitude limit is about 4 percent of the spin-down value.
prerequisites: continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars
concepts.notes: 4 percent in amplitude corresponds to about 0.16 percent of the energy, slightly above the text's 'less than 0.1%'.

concepts.name: r-mode instability
concepts.definition: A gravitational-radiation-driven instability of rotational (Rossby-type) oscillation modes in rapidly spinning neutron stars, in which emission of gravitational waves makes the mode grow (a CFS-type instability).
concepts.how_introduced: Named in a single sentence as a possible strong continuous-wave mechanism and, later, as a possible mechanism in accreting X-ray pulsars.
prerequisites: continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars

concepts.name: burst search
concepts.definition: A search for short gravitational-wave transients that makes minimal assumptions about waveform shape, requiring the signal to stand above the noise (or to match generic wavelets) and relying on coincidence, coherence or external triggers for confidence.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by supernova core collapse, whose chaotic dynamics prevent waveform prediction; generalized to any unanticipated source; implemented with sine-Gaussian template banks.
concepts.notes: GW150914 was first flagged by an online burst search.

concepts.name: core-collapse supernova gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Gravitational radiation from the non-spherical dynamics of a collapsing stellar core and proto-neutron star; together with neutrinos it is the only direct probe of the core, but predicted amplitudes are small and waveforms are stochastic, so only Galactic or nearby events are likely detectable.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as Weber's original goal; simulations suggest small amplitudes with possible spectral features; neutrino timing would anchor a search since the optical display appears hours later.

concepts.name: cosmic strings
concepts.definition: Hypothetical one-dimensional topological defects formed in early-Universe phase transitions in some field theories; their oscillations, cusps and reconnections would emit gravitational-wave bursts with a characteristic spectral shape.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as a speculative burst source and a possible exotic dark component; searched for routinely with a spectral-shape filter.

concepts.name: stochastic gravitational wave background
concepts.definition: A random superposition of gravitational waves from very many unresolved sources arriving from all directions, statistically described by its mean square amplitude or spectral energy density rather than a waveform. The astrophysical background comes from recent populations such as binary black holes and white dwarfs; a cosmological background would be a relic of the very early Universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by analogy with the cosmic microwave background, emphasising that the Universe has been transparent to gravitational waves since the beginning; Figure 12.2 shows the predicted binary black hole background against LIGO sensitivity; later its detection method is derived.
concepts.notes: Pulsar timing arrays reported evidence for a nHz background in 2023, after this edition was written.

concepts.name: energy density parameter of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: The energy density of a gravitational-wave background (usually per logarithmic frequency interval) divided by the critical energy density of the Universe; used because a random field has no characteristic amplitude but does have a mean energy density proportional to f^2 times the mean square strain.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified from randomness (no single h) and homogeneity (same everywhere); quoted limits Omega_gw < 1.7e-7 from O1, about 1e-9 at LIGO design, and LISA reach near 1e-10.
concepts.notes: The book does not define Omega_gw per logarithmic frequency explicitly.

concepts.name: cross-correlation search
concepts.definition: Detecting a stochastic background by multiplying the outputs of two detectors whose instrumental noises are independent but which see the same gravitational-wave field, and summing over time; the noise products average to zero while the common signal accumulates.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in 12.2 with the fourth-root sensitivity scaling, then derived in 12.3 for two co-located aligned detectors with white noise.

concepts.name: pulsar timing array
concepts.definition: A set of millisecond pulsars whose pulse arrival times are monitored for years; a nHz gravitational wave perturbs the arrival times, and correlations between pulsars reveal a background or individual supermassive black-hole binaries.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the nHz band detector, expected to see the supermassive binary background first, and likened to a correlation search where each pulsar is a detector.

concepts.name: polarization basis tensors
concepts.definition: Symmetric traceless tensors in the plane transverse to the propagation direction, built from an orthonormal sky-plane basis: e+ = eX eX - eY eY and ex = eX eY + eY eX; any TT wave's spatial metric perturbation is h+ e+ + hx ex.
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed with outer products so that the wave can be described in a frame independent of any particular detector.
concepts.notes: Rotating the sky-plane basis by an angle psi mixes h+ and hx with angle 2 psi.

concepts.name: detector tensor
concepts.definition: For an L-shaped interferometer with unit arm vectors e_x and e_y, the tensor d = L(e_x e_x - e_y e_y), whose full contraction with the wave tensor gives the difference in arm-length changes.
concepts.how_introduced: Built in parallel with the wave's basis tensors so that the response becomes a single coordinate-free contraction; tested for special directions in Exercise 12.3.
concepts.notes: As printed, d contains L and no factor 1/2, so d:h equals twice the physical arm-length difference (each arm changes by h L/2); conventional definitions include the 1/2. The dimensionless response is d:h/L in the book's notation.

concepts.name: antenna pattern functions
concepts.definition: The geometric coefficients F+ = d:e+/L and Fx = d:ex/L giving the detector strain delta = F+ h+ + Fx hx; they depend on the source direction relative to the detector's zenith and arms and on the chosen orientation of the sky-plane basis.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by splitting the double contraction into polarization parts; emphasised that a single source has different angles, hence different F values, at each detector.
concepts.notes: The book says F depends only on theta and phi; it also depends on the polarization angle of the sky basis, as the text itself uses when rotating that basis. Standard results: F+ = (1/2)(1+cos^2 theta)cos 2phi cos 2psi - cos theta sin 2phi sin 2psi, Fx = (1/2)(1+cos^2 theta)cos 2phi sin 2psi + cos theta sin 2phi cos 2psi.

concepts.name: antenna power pattern
concepts.definition: The polarization-averaged directional sensitivity F+^2 + Fx^2 of a detector, largest for waves arriving from the zenith or nadir and zero for waves arriving in the detector plane along a bisector of the arms (in the plane along an arm it is a quarter of the zenith value); for a network of identical detectors the patterns add. With the conventional detector-tensor normalization the zenith value is 1; the book's literal Eq. 12.8 would make it 4, and Figure 12.4 is drawn normalized.
concepts.how_introduced: Plotted as 3D surfaces for a single interferometer and for the two LIGOs plus Virgo in Figure 12.4, with the caution that long signals see a rotating pattern.
concepts.notes: GW170817 arrived near a null of Virgo's pattern, which itself helped localization.

concepts.name: amplitude spectral density of detector noise
concepts.definition: The square root of the noise power spectral density of the strain output, in units of 1/sqrt(Hz), giving the r.m.s. noise amplitude per unit bandwidth as a function of frequency; comparing it with signal spectra shows which sources a detector can see.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented through Figure 12.5's LIGO and Virgo curves for successive observing runs, with the caption explaining why the square root is plotted.

concepts.name: Gaussian detector noise
concepts.definition: Noise whose value in each frequency bin (or sample) is drawn from a zero-mean normal distribution with a time-independent variance; expected when many independent noise mechanisms add, by the central limit theorem.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by the central limit theorem applied to thermal vibrations of atoms, photon arrivals and seismic jostling; contrasted with glitches.

concepts.name: shot noise
concepts.definition: Noise from the random (Poisson) arrival of photons at the photodetector; its relative size falls as the inverse square root of the number of photons, so it dominates interferometer sensitivity at high frequencies and is reduced by more laser power, at the cost of radiation-pressure and heating noise.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained heuristically: higher frequencies need shorter sampling intervals with fewer photons each, giving a rise with frequency; then used in design trade-offs.
concepts.notes: In real Fabry-Perot interferometers the high-frequency shot-noise rise in strain spectral density is roughly proportional to f, set by the arm-cavity response, not the f^(1/2) of this sampling heuristic.

concepts.name: thermal noise
concepts.definition: Brownian motion of mirror surfaces, coatings and suspension fibres driven by their temperature; it limits sensitivity in the most sensitive mid band (tens to hundreds of Hz) and produces narrow resonance lines from suspension modes.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the mid-band floor in Figure 12.5; motivates cryogenic mirrors in KAGRA.

concepts.name: seismic noise
concepts.definition: Ground vibrations transmitted to the test masses through their suspensions, increasingly hard to isolate at low frequencies and responsible for the steep low-frequency wall of ground-based sensitivity curves.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the reason noise rises below a few tens of Hz.

concepts.name: Newtonian noise
concepts.definition: Fluctuating tidal forces on the test masses from time-varying local mass distributions (passing seismic waves, atmospheric changes, moving people or vehicles); because it couples exactly like a gravitational wave it cannot be shielded, only reduced by going underground or into space.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the limit for third-generation ground detectors and the principal reason LISA must fly: below 1 Hz the Earth is gravitationally too noisy.

concepts.name: glitches
concepts.definition: Short, loud, non-Gaussian noise transients of varied morphology, arising from malfunctioning electronics and control systems, which come and go in time and can mimic astrophysical bursts; they dominate the background of short-duration searches.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with stationary Gaussian noise; later drives the need for coincidence, time slides and null-stream vetoes; a real glitch overlapped GW170817 in Livingston.

concepts.name: matched filtering
concepts.definition: Correlating detector data with a predicted waveform (template) at all time offsets; for known signal shape in Gaussian noise this linear statistic maximizes signal-to-noise ratio, peaks at the arrival time with height proportional to amplitude times the template's squared norm, and allows detection of signals far below the raw noise level.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by GW170817 being invisible in raw data yet highly significant; derived in a toy model of sampled white Gaussian noise plus a scaled, shifted template, compared with naive threshold crossing; historical origin in radar and in Kafka's 1977 bar-detector proposal.
concepts.notes: With coloured noise the correlation must be weighted by the inverse noise spectrum, which the book only mentions (frequency domain, Exercise 12.4).

concepts.name: template bank
concepts.definition: A discrete set of model waveforms spanning the source parameter space (masses, spins) densely enough that any real signal matches some template closely; the template with the largest filter output estimates the parameters.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed because binary masses range widely; templates use post-Newtonian inspirals joined to numerical-relativity mergers; computing cost handled with FFTs.
concepts.notes: Current banks assume quasi-circular orbits because inspiral radiation circularizes most binaries; the book notes that searches for eccentric systems (e.g. from triples) are planned.

concepts.name: white noise
concepts.definition: Noise with no statistical correlation between different times, so that the covariance of samples is sigma^2 times a Kronecker delta and the power spectrum is flat.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted as a simplifying assumption to expose the power of matched filtering, immediately flagged as untrue for real detectors (Figure 12.5).

concepts.name: signal-to-noise ratio
concepts.definition: The expected value of a detection statistic in the presence of a signal divided by its standard deviation in noise alone; thresholds on it set detection confidence, and for a network the matched-filter SNRs add in quadrature.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined implicitly through filter mean and variance; applied to matched filtering, correlation searches and Table 12.1's network SNR column.

concepts.name: square-root-of-cycles gain of matched filtering
concepts.definition: Coherently integrating a known oscillating signal lowers the minimum detectable amplitude, relative to its peak value, by roughly the square root of the number of signal cycles; the same random-walk scaling appears in repeated measurements and continuous-wave searches (sensitivity improves as the square root of observation time).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived for a pure sinusoid (squared norm B^2 N/2), then reinterpreted as cycles rather than samples via a resampling argument; applied to explain why long neutron-star chirps and pulsar signals benefit most.

concepts.name: detection range and volume
concepts.definition: Because strain falls off as the reciprocal of source distance, the farthest detectable source lies at a distance that scales as one over the smallest amplitude a search can pick out, and the surveyed volume (hence the expected rate for uniformly spread sources) grows as the cube of that distance.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to translate the matched-filter gain into N^(3/2) more detections, to explain Figure 12.5's binary-neutron-star range legends, and the rapid growth of catalog sizes.

concepts.name: intrinsic and extrinsic parameters
concepts.definition: Intrinsic parameters (component masses, spins) describe the source itself and shape the waveform, so a single detector can estimate them; extrinsic parameters (sky position, distance, inclination, polarization angle, arrival time) describe its relation to the observer and require a network.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced when moving from detection to measurement; ordered by accuracy (chirp mass best, others worse by five or more).

concepts.name: Bayesian parameter estimation
concepts.definition: Combining a likelihood of the data given model parameters with prior probabilities (astrophysical and instrumental) to obtain a posterior distribution, which yields best estimates and credible intervals for each parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the practical method behind parameter values and uncertainties; its output is shown in Figure 12.6 for H0; contrasted with the frequentist significance discussion.

concepts.name: polarization reconstruction with two detectors
concepts.definition: Given a known source direction and a common wave-phase time, the responses of two non-aligned detectors form a linear 2x2 system in h+ and hx, which is inverted using the determinant of the antenna-factor matrix.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out explicitly for a sky position known from a gamma-ray burst, after shifting each detector's time to a common reference.
concepts.notes: Fails when the two detectors are nearly aligned (determinant near zero), as for the two LIGO sites.

concepts.name: inclination from polarization ratio
concepts.definition: For a circular binary, the plus and cross amplitudes in the basis aligned with the projected orbit are in quadrature with ratio (1 + cos^2 iota)/(2 cos iota); rotating the sky basis until the reconstructed polarizations are 90 degrees out of phase and measuring their amplitude ratio gives the inclination iota.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the edge-on special case (linear polarization, one component vanishes for the right rotation), then generalized to elliptical polarization using Eq. 9.100.

concepts.name: distance-inclination degeneracy
concepts.definition: For nearly face-on binaries the amplitude changes only at second order in inclination, so a signal can be fit almost equally well by a closer, more inclined source or a farther face-on one, inflating distance errors; since face-on systems are loudest, they dominate detected samples.
concepts.how_introduced: Follows from the flatness of the amplitude ratio near iota = 0 (quantified in Exercise 12.7: a 1 percent ratio error allows iota up to 30 degrees); returns as the main error in the GW170817 H0 posterior; broken by higher harmonics in GW190521 and GW190814.

concepts.name: higher harmonics in binary waveforms
concepts.definition: Gravitational radiation from a binary beyond the leading quadrupole at twice the orbital frequency, arising from post-Newtonian corrections and mass asymmetry; they have different frequencies and angular dependences, so detecting them improves inclination, polarization and distance estimates.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the cure for the distance-inclination degeneracy, then shown in action in GW190521 (distance revised from 4.1 to 5.3 Gpc) and GW190814 (large mass ratio).

concepts.name: false alarm probability
concepts.definition: The probability that noise alone exceeds a detection threshold; for zero-mean Gaussian noise and a threshold of a standard deviations it is 2 times the integral of the unit normal density from a to infinity, bounded above by (twice) phi(a)/a, which becomes accurate for large a.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to answer 'what is a detection?', converted into expected false-alarm counts using realistic sample numbers.
concepts.notes: The printed bounds in Eq. 12.29 omit the factor 2 of Eq. 12.27, although the quoted numbers include it.

concepts.name: trials factor
concepts.definition: When a statistic is evaluated many independent times (samples, templates, sky positions), the chance that at least one noise value exceeds a threshold grows with the number of trials, so thresholds must be raised accordingly.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown numerically: 5 sigma is common in a year of data; 6.5 is needed per filter sample; 8 is needed with 10,000 templates.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the term 'trials factor' but the argument is exactly this.

concepts.name: coincidence analysis
concepts.definition: Accepting a candidate only when triggers occur in two or more detectors within a time window set by the light-travel time between sites (plus a margin), which suppresses uncorrelated glitches.
concepts.how_introduced: Justified by the difficulty of setting safe single-detector thresholds against glitches; the reason LIGO was built as two detectors.

concepts.name: time slides
concepts.definition: Estimating the false-alarm background by artificially shifting one detector's data relative to another by more than the physical coincidence window and repeating the search many times; any coincidences found are necessarily accidental, measuring the combined glitch and Gaussian background rate.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as how LIGO-Virgo determines residual coincident-glitch rates and thus the false-alarm rates in Table 12.1.

concepts.name: false alarm rate
concepts.definition: The expected rate (per year) at which noise, including glitches, would produce a candidate at least as strong as a given event; small values indicate high significance, and catalogs accept events below a chosen FAR threshold.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in Table 12.1 and used to discuss GWTC-2's threshold of two per year and the trade-off between purity and completeness.

concepts.name: likelihood ratio
concepts.definition: The ratio of the probability of the data under a signal-plus-noise hypothesis to that under noise alone (or between two signal models); thresholding it gives the optimal Neyman-Pearson detection statistic, and Bayes factors compare models such as tensor versus scalar polarization.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the deeper Bayesian alternative to the frequentist treatment; Bayes factors of 1000 and 200 quoted for GW170814's polarization test.

concepts.name: coherent network analysis
concepts.definition: Combining the data streams of all detectors, with appropriate time shifts and antenna factors for a hypothesized direction, before applying any threshold, so that the consistency of amplitudes and phases expected from a single two-polarization wave is exploited.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with coincidence, which throws away amplitude-consistency information; attributed to Gursel and Tinto, Bose et al., and Finn, with the aperture-synthesis analogy.

concepts.name: null stream
concepts.definition: A linear combination of the (time-aligned) outputs of three or more detectors, weighted by antenna-factor determinants for an assumed source direction, in which any gravitational-wave signal from that direction cancels identically, leaving only instrumental noise and glitches; a network of N detectors has N - 2 null streams.
concepts.how_introduced: Predicted by counting (two polarization functions versus three data streams), derived by eliminating h+ and hx (Exercise 12.8), then applied to glitch vetoes, glitch subtraction, source localization and calibration checks; LISA's Sagnac combination is an example.

concepts.name: detector calibration
concepts.definition: Establishing, across all frequencies, the conversion between a detector's raw output and true gravitational strain in amplitude and phase; errors bias amplitudes and hence distances, and inconsistent calibrations spoil null streams.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as one of the hardest operational problems, with the idea of calibrating one detector precisely and transferring calibration via null streams and well-modelled binary waveforms.

concepts.name: Doppler modulation of continuous-wave signals
concepts.definition: Periodic frequency and phase modulation of a monochromatic gravitational wave caused by the detector's accelerated motion (Earth's spin and orbit), depending on source direction; it smears the signal over many frequency bins once the observation exceeds a critical duration.
concepts.how_introduced: Critical time estimated by equating the accumulated Doppler drift f Omega^2 R T / c to the frequency resolution 2/T, giving about 70 minutes at 1 kHz for Earth's rotation.
prerequisites: continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars

concepts.name: barycentric demodulation
aliases: resampling to the solar system barycenter
concepts.definition: Undoing the direction-dependent Doppler modulation by re-sampling the detector's time series onto a clock that would tick uniformly for an unaccelerated observer at the Solar System's centre of mass, using the light-travel delay n.d/c for the trial sky direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Described in words for the optimal search and quantified in Exercise 12.9, which also treats spin-down by an analogous time remapping.

concepts.name: angular resolution by orbital aperture synthesis
concepts.definition: A long observation of a continuous signal lets the detector's motion across Earth's orbit act like a telescope of diameter 2R, giving a diffraction-limited angular resolution of order lambda/2R (about 2e-6 rad at 1 kHz for half an orbit), just as pulsar timing localizes radio pulsars.
concepts.how_introduced: Deduced from the direction dependence of the Doppler pattern; turned into a count of about 3e12 sky patches that each need their own search.

concepts.name: computational cost of all-sky continuous-wave searches
concepts.definition: Because each resolvable sky patch and each distinguishable spin-down rate needs a separate demodulation and Fourier transform, an optimal coherent all-sky search over months of data requires vastly more computation than exists, forcing semi-coherent, suboptimal strategies.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from sky-patch counts plus spin-down bins and estimated in Exercise 12.9 in floating-point operations and supercomputer-equivalents; contrasted with targeted searches of known pulsars.
prerequisites: angular resolution by orbital aperture synthesis

concepts.name: Sagnac null stream
concepts.definition: For LISA's triangular constellation, a combination of the three interferometer outputs that is insensitive to gravitational waves at low frequencies, providing an in-situ measurement of instrumental noise against which an excess due to a stochastic background can be judged.
concepts.how_introduced: Explains how a single space mission, which cannot cross-correlate independent detectors because its interferometers share arms, can still search for a background.

concepts.name: sine-Gaussian burst templates
concepts.definition: Generic filters formed by a sinusoid multiplied by a Gaussian envelope a few cycles wide; banks spanning central frequency and width can partially match many unmodelled short transients.
concepts.how_introduced: Proposed as a minimal-assumption compromise between pure excess-power searches and full matched filtering; GW150914's late-time waveform resembles one.

concepts.name: GW150914
concepts.definition: The first directly detected gravitational-wave signal, from a binary black hole merger (about 36 and 29 solar masses in the source frame, final mass 62, luminosity distance about 410 Mpc), recorded by both LIGO detectors in September 2015 and announced in February 2016.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the chapter's opening image, as a check on the merger-frequency and ringdown estimates, as an example visible without matched filtering, and told as a discovery story in 12.4. In 12.4 the book also explains why the components are called black holes: their masses plus the compactness implied by the highest orbital frequency leave no conventional alternative; horizonless exotic objects need unobserved physics, and a direct test would be measuring the remnant's quasi-normal ringing, which the collaboration did not claim.
concepts.notes: The overview gives 14 September 2015 (correct, 09:50:45 UTC), while 12.4 speaks of 15 September and local times one hour earlier than daylight-saving clocks would show.

concepts.name: event naming convention
concepts.definition: Gravitational-wave events are named GW followed by the two-digit year, month and day of detection in Universal Time; later catalogs append the UTC time of day to distinguish multiple events on one date.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained in a footnote at the first use of GW150914.
concepts.notes: Footnote dropped by the text export; recovered from the page render.

concepts.name: graviton mass bound from dispersion
concepts.definition: A nonzero graviton mass would make gravitational-wave speed depend on frequency, so different parts of a chirp would arrive with accumulated relative delays over the propagation distance; absence of such distortion bounds the mass (1.2e-22 eV from GW150914).
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as one of the waveform-consistency tests of general relativity, with the caveat that static-field bounds are stronger.
concepts.notes: The text says shorter wavelengths travel faster; for a massive graviton the group velocity is closer to c at higher frequency, consistent with that statement.

concepts.name: polarization test of general relativity
concepts.definition: Checking whether the responses of three or more differently oriented detectors are consistent with only the two tensor polarizations of general relativity, as opposed to scalar (breathing) or vector modes; GW170814 favoured pure tensor over pure scalar and pure vector with Bayes factors of about 1000 and 200.
concepts.how_introduced: Enabled by the first three-detector event; the book stresses that realistic alternatives add modes rather than replace tensor ones, which the data could not yet test.

concepts.name: GW170817
concepts.definition: The first detected binary neutron star merger (component masses about 1.44 and 1.28 solar masses, chirp mass 1.186, distance about 40 Mpc), accompanied 1.7 s later by a short gamma-ray burst and followed by a kilonova in NGC 4993; the birth of gravitational-wave multimessenger astronomy.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced early as a weak-but-significant matched-filter example and a glitch-plus-signal case; told in detail in 12.4 including localization, H0, tidal limits and r-process results.
concepts.notes: Text gives 31 square degrees for the initial localization; Table 12.1 lists 16 from the final analysis.

concepts.name: standard siren
concepts.definition: Using a compact binary's chirp, whose frequency evolution fixes its intrinsic luminosity, to infer the luminosity distance directly from the observed amplitude, once the inclination (and sky position) are known; no cosmic distance ladder is required.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Section 9.6 and used for GW170817's 40 plus or minus 8 Mpc, with inclination identified as the dominant uncertainty.

concepts.name: Hubble-Lemaitre constant from gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Dividing the Hubble-flow recession velocity of a host galaxy (from its redshift, corrected for peculiar velocity) by the standard-siren luminosity distance gives H0; without an identified host, the redshifts of all galaxies in the localization volume can be combined statistically.
concepts.how_introduced: GW170817's posterior (Figure 12.6) lies between Planck and SH0ES values but is broad because of inclination; radio jet constraints later gave 70.3 plus or minus 5; GW190814 illustrated the host-less statistical method (Schutz 1986).

concepts.name: relativistic jet and viewing angle
concepts.definition: A narrow (roughly 5-20 degree) ultra-relativistic outflow launched along the merger's angular momentum axis powers short gamma-ray bursts; an observer slightly off-axis sees a weaker burst, and since the jet axis coincides with the orbital axis, jet-angle measurements constrain the gravitational-wave inclination.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised by GRB170817A being ordinary in brightness though very near; radio imaging later placed the viewing angle at 14-28 degrees.
prerequisites: short gamma-ray bursts from neutron star mergers

concepts.name: tidal deformability
concepts.definition: The response coefficient relating a star's induced quadrupole moment to an applied external tidal field; it depends on the nuclear equation of state and speeds up the final inspiral of neutron stars, leaving a phase imprint in the last orbits.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a way to learn nuclear physics from GW170817; only upper limits so far, excluding some very stiff equations of state.

concepts.name: r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers
concepts.definition: Production of heavy neutron-rich nuclei (gold, platinum, thorium, uranium and others) in neutron-rich ejecta from compact mergers; spectra of the GW170817 kilonova support mergers as a major site.
concepts.how_introduced: Told with a vivid picture of neutron-star matter breaking into ever smaller neutron-rich chunks, historical credit to Lattimer and Schramm and Eichler et al., and a connection from uranium and thorium heating to plate tectonics and Earth's magnetic field.
concepts.notes: The book attributes heavy-element formation to fission; the standard picture is rapid neutron capture onto seed nuclei (with fission recycling only for the heaviest nuclei).

concepts.name: GW190425
concepts.definition: A likely binary neutron star merger with total mass about 3.4 solar masses, heavier than any Galactic double neutron star, detected significantly only in LIGO-Livingston (Hanford offline, Virgo weak), hence poorly localized and without counterpart.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as an outlier challenging formation models and as a single-detector detection.

concepts.name: GW190521
concepts.definition: An unusually massive binary black hole merger (about 85 plus 65 solar masses, remnant about 142) at several Gpc, in band for only about four cycles, whose remnant is an intermediate-mass black hole and whose primary lies where stellar collapse is not expected to form black holes.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to discuss hierarchical mergers, a candidate AGN-disk flare counterpart driven by the remnant's recoil, and the role of higher multipoles in distance estimation.
concepts.notes: Table 12.1 prints its distance as 5.3 in a Mpc column; it is 5.3 Gpc.

concepts.name: GW190814
concepts.definition: A merger of a roughly 23 solar-mass black hole with a 2.6 solar-mass compact object lying in the lower mass gap, with the most extreme mass ratio (about 9:1) seen by 2021; its higher harmonics constrained inclination and enabled a statistical H0 estimate.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a mass-gap puzzle and a demonstration of what asymmetric binaries add to distance measurements.

concepts.name: intermediate-mass black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole with mass between roughly 100 and 1e5 solar masses, between stellar remnants and galactic-nucleus black holes, for which pre-2019 evidence was sparse.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 11 and shown to be produced by GW190521.

concepts.name: hierarchical black hole mergers
concepts.definition: Formation of a heavy black hole by the merger of lighter black holes, followed by a later merger of the product with another object, e.g. in dense clusters or triples; proposed to explain black holes too massive to form directly from stellar collapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Suggested for GW190521's 85 solar-mass primary, with the open question of triple versus sequential binary histories.
concepts.notes: The book does not name the pair-instability mass gap that motivates this.

concepts.name: lower mass gap
aliases: mass gap between neutron stars and black holes
concepts.definition: The apparent scarcity, in pre-LIGO electromagnetic observations, of compact objects between about 2.2 solar masses (heaviest known pulsars) and about 6 solar masses (lightest X-ray-binary black holes).
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to explain why GW190814's 2.6 solar-mass companion, and perhaps GW190425's primary, are surprising.

concepts.name: gravitational recoil
concepts.definition: The linear momentum given to a merger remnant by asymmetric emission of gravitational waves in the final orbits and merger, potentially hundreds of km/s or more; in a gaseous environment the moving remnant might produce an electromagnetic flare.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the mechanism behind the proposed AGN-disk flare associated with GW190521, with a predicted repeat flare as a test.

concepts.name: gravitational wave transient catalog
concepts.definition: Periodic LIGO-Virgo(-KAGRA) releases listing all confident compact-binary detections of an observing period with their parameters, used for population statistics, rates and combined tests of general relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented with event counts per run and a discussion of lowering significance thresholds to avoid discarding real events.
concepts.notes: Dated: GWTC-3 (2021) and later O4 releases have since greatly extended the catalog.

concepts.name: redshifted masses
concepts.definition: Because cosmological redshift stretches all timescales, a binary at redshift z is observed with masses (1+z) times its source-frame masses; catalogs quote source-frame masses and luminosity distances.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in Table 12.1's note referring to Eq. 9.163, and implicitly in using a detector-frame 68 solar-mass remnant for the ringdown estimate.

concepts.name: open gravitational wave data
aliases: citizen science in gravitational wave analysis
concepts.definition: Public release of calibrated strain data and event audio, enabling independent analyses (which have promoted marginal events to detections) and volunteer projects such as Einstein@Home for pulsar searches and Gravity Spy for glitch classification.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the further-observations discussion of non-collaboration detections and in the bibliography's resource list.

concepts.name: merger remnant outcomes
concepts.definition: What is left after compact objects touch depends on the pair: two neutron stars form a very massive star that probably collapses to a black hole unless the nuclear equation of state can support it; a neutron star plus black hole may briefly keep matter in a disk before becoming a nearly vacuum black hole; two black holes form a distorted black hole that rings down to Kerr, most likely without electromagnetic emission.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the reason a merger signal does not end at first contact, leading straight into the ringdown estimate and its GW150914 check.

concepts.name: targeted continuous-wave search
concepts.definition: A search for gravitational waves from a neutron star whose sky position (and usually spin frequency) is known from electromagnetic timing, so demodulation is fixed and only spin-down parameters (for young pulsars even the second frequency derivative) must be scanned; accreting X-ray pulsars such as Sco X-1 add poorly known binary-orbit parameters.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with blind all-sky searches as far cheaper and somewhat more sensitive; the book adds that because a Doppler-modulated signal is unlike any terrestrial artefact, such searches usually run on the single most sensitive detector and confirm candidates in the others.
concepts.notes: No detections by mid-2021; Crab limit about 4 percent of its spin-down value.

key_equations.name: Frequency versus orbital phase remaining
key_equations.meaning: Gravitational-wave frequency (twice orbital) of a leading-order inspiral when psi radians of orbital phase remain, from inverting Eq. 9.159 with f = omega/pi.
key_equations.symbols: f_gw = omega/pi with omega the orbital angular frequency; M = chirp mass; psi = orbital phase to merger

key_equations.name: Merger frequency estimate
key_equations.meaning: Setting psi = pi (half an orbit left) gives the frequency above which little power is recorded; 130 Hz for GW150914, a few kHz for binary neutron stars, 20 Hz at a chirp mass of about 200 solar masses.

key_equations.name: Scaled time to merger
key_equations.meaning: Remaining inspiral time from a given gravitational-wave frequency; about 9-10 months from 30 mHz for a 30 solar-mass chirp mass, 2.5 minutes from 20 Hz for two 1.4 solar-mass neutron stars.
key_equations.symbols: M = chirp mass; f_gw = gravitational-wave frequency

key_equations.name: Ringdown frequency estimate
key_equations.meaning: Characteristic quasi-normal ringing frequency of a black hole of mass M, from omega about 0.5/M; about 230 Hz for a 68 solar-mass detector-frame remnant.
key_equations.symbols: M = remnant mass; here f = omega/(2 pi)

key_equations.name: Continuous-wave strain from a spinning neutron star
key_equations.meaning: Order-of-magnitude strain along the spin axis from a star with fractional non-axisymmetry epsilon; about 1e-26 for I = 1e38 kg m^2, f = 60 Hz, r = 1 kpc, epsilon = 1e-6 (after restoring G/c^4).
key_equations.symbols: epsilon = asymmetry; Omega = 2 pi f spin angular frequency; I_NS = moment of inertia; r = distance; geometrized units

key_equations.name: Continuous-wave sensitivity versus observation time
key_equations.meaning: Coherent integration of a monochromatic signal lowers the detectable amplitude as the inverse square root of observing time; reaching 1e-26 from a 1e-22 broadband level needs about 1e8 cycles. (The book prints h_min proportional to T^(1/2); the exponent sign is corrected here, since the text says sensitivity improves with time.)

key_equations.name: Stochastic-background sensitivity versus observation time
key_equations.meaning: Cross-correlation lowers the detectable r.m.s. background amplitude only as the fourth root of observing time. (Printed in the book as T^(1/4); sign corrected here.)

key_equations.name: Polarization basis tensors
key_equations.latex: \mathbf e_+=\hat e^R_x\otimes\hat e^R_x-\hat e^R_y\otimes\hat e^R_y,\qquad \mathbf e_\times=\hat e^R_x\otimes\hat e^R_y+\hat e^R_y\otimes\hat e^R_x
key_equations.meaning: Plus and cross tensors built from an orthonormal basis in the plane of the sky, independent of any detector.
