key_equations.symbols: e^R_x, e^R_y = sky-plane basis vectors perpendicular to the propagation direction N

key_equations.name: Wave tensor
key_equations.meaning: The spatial TT metric perturbation of the incoming wave written in the sky-plane polarization basis.

key_equations.name: Detector tensor
key_equations.meaning: Encodes an L-shaped interferometer's arm directions and length in one tensor.
key_equations.symbols: L = arm length; e_x, e_y = unit vectors along the arms

key_equations.name: Interferometer response as a double contraction
key_equations.meaning: The difference between the stretchings of the two arms is the full contraction of detector and wave tensors, valid for any direction and polarization. Normalization check (ours): because a TT wave changes an arm of length L by (1/2) h L, the literal d:h with d = L(e_x e_x - e_y e_y) equals twice the arm-length difference; conventional treatments put a factor 1/2 in the detector tensor. Ratios such as those in Exercise 12.3 and Figure 12.4 are unaffected.
key_equations.symbols: Delta_int = arm-length difference; ':' = double inner product

key_equations.name: Strain response with antenna patterns
key_equations.meaning: Detector strain separates into geometry-only antenna factors times the two polarization waveforms.
key_equations.symbols: theta, phi = source direction in detector-based spherical coordinates (zenith = pole); F also depends on the sky-basis orientation

key_equations.name: Antenna power pattern
key_equations.meaning: Polarization-averaged directional sensitivity plotted in Figure 12.4; network patterns add for identical detectors.

key_equations.name: Data model: noise plus shifted template
key_equations.meaning: Sampled detector output containing Gaussian noise and a signal of known shape, unknown amplitude A and unknown arrival index D.
key_equations.symbols: x_j = data (M samples); n_j = zero-mean Gaussian noise, std sigma; w_j = template (N samples, zero outside); D = arrival sample

key_equations.name: Naive threshold-crossing criterion
key_equations.meaning: Watching raw data, a signal is noticed only if its peak value exceeds the noise level; w_K is the template maximum.

key_equations.name: Filter output (correlation with template)
key_equations.meaning: Slide the template along the data and take the inner product at each lag k (called a convolution in the book; it is a cross-correlation).

key_equations.name: Filter output split into noise and signal parts
key_equations.meaning: Linear in the noise, so the output is Gaussian; the second term is deterministic.

key_equations.name: Mean filter output
key_equations.meaning: The expected output is the template's autocorrelation, scaled by A and centred at the true arrival index. The book's middle expression carries an extra factor A and writes x where the signal part is meant; only the final equality is right.

key_equations.name: Peak mean output
key_equations.meaning: At k = D the mean output equals amplitude times the template's squared norm.

key_equations.name: Variance of the filter output
key_equations.meaning: Definition of variance applied to the filter statistic; only the noise-noise term survives.

key_equations.name: Surviving noise term
key_equations.meaning: The variance is the noise covariance weighted by the template at the chosen lag. Written here with the template weights restored; the book prints only the double sum of noise covariances, var[n] = sum_j sum_j' <n_j n_j'>, dropping the w factors.

key_equations.name: White-noise covariance
key_equations.meaning: No correlation between distinct samples; a simplification real detector noise violates.

key_equations.name: Filter variance for white noise
key_equations.meaning: The noise in the filter output is sigma times the template norm, the same at every lag. Corrected form. The book prints sigma^2 (w*w)_(k-D), which agrees with sigma^2 ||w||^2 only at the peak lag k = D, so Eq. 12.20 is unaffected.

key_equations.name: Matched-filter detection threshold
key_equations.meaning: Signal-to-noise ratio A||w||/sigma reaches one at this amplitude: the template's integrated norm replaces its peak value, so long signals are detectable at much lower amplitude.

key_equations.name: Norm of a sinusoidal template
key_equations.latex: B^2\sum_j\sin^2(\omega\Delta t\,j)=\tfrac12 B^2\sum_j\big[1-\cos(2\omega\Delta t\,j)\big]\approx \tfrac12 B^2 N
key_equations.meaning: Over many cycles the oscillating term averages away, leaving half the sample count.
key_equations.symbols: B = template amplitude; N = number of template samples; Delta t = sampling interval

key_equations.name: Matched-filter gain for a sinusoid
key_equations.meaning: Compared with Eq. 12.12, the threshold drops by a factor proportional to the square root of the signal length (properly, of its number of cycles); range improves by that factor, volume by its cube.

key_equations.name: Effective filtered noise level
key_equations.meaning: Amplitude at which a matched-filtered signal has SNR = 1: an effective noise level for detectors.

key_equations.name: Two-detector responses at common time
key_equations.meaning: Each detector's strain, time-shifted to a common wave phase, is a different linear combination of the same two polarizations.
key_equations.symbols: T = common reference time; subscripts 1, 2 label detectors; F evaluated at each detector's own angles

key_equations.name: Two-detector response matrix
key_equations.meaning: Matrix mapping (h+, hx) to (delta1, delta2); the subscript names the detector pair, not matrix indices.

key_equations.name: Inverse response matrix
key_equations.meaning: Standard 2x2 inverse; singular when the detectors are aligned.

key_equations.name: Polarization reconstruction
key_equations.meaning: Two non-aligned detectors recover both polarization waveforms for a known sky position.

key_equations.name: Polarization amplitude ratio and inclination
key_equations.meaning: In the sky basis where the two polarizations are in quadrature, their amplitude ratio fixes the orbital inclination; it tends to 1 face-on and diverges edge-on.
key_equations.symbols: iota = inclination of orbital angular momentum to line of sight

key_equations.name: Inclination from the ratio (Exercise 12.7)
key_equations.meaning: Solving Eq. 12.26; the quartic flatness near face-on shows why inclination (and therefore distance) is poorly measured for loud face-on systems.

key_equations.name: Two-sided Gaussian false-alarm probability
key_equations.meaning: Probability that a zero-mean Gaussian noise sample exceeds a sigma in magnitude.
key_equations.symbols: a = threshold in units of sigma

key_equations.name: Unit normal density
key_equations.meaning: Gaussian probability density with unit standard deviation.

key_equations.name: Gaussian tail bounds
key_equations.meaning: The upper bound approaches the exact tail for large a and gives the quoted numbers: 6e-7 at a = 5, 2e-9 at 6, 8e-11 at 6.5, 1.3e-15 at 8. The factor 2 is restored here: the book prints the bounds as a phi(a)/(1+a^2) and phi(a)/a, although its quoted probabilities include the two-sided factor.

key_equations.name: Three-detector responses
key_equations.meaning: Three data streams depending on only two unknown waveforms, so one combination must be signal-free.

key_equations.name: Null combination of signal strains
key_equations.meaning: The gravitational-wave-induced strains in three detectors satisfy an exact linear identity for a given source direction (Exercise 12.8).

key_equations.name: Pair determinants
key_equations.meaning: Weights of the null combination; antisymmetric in a and b.

key_equations.name: Null stream
key_equations.meaning: The same combination applied to real outputs x = n + delta contains only noise and glitches; used as a veto, for localization and for calibration checks.

key_equations.name: Doppler frequency drift from detector acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Frequency change accumulated in time T from circular motion of radius R and angular velocity Omega, compared with the frequency resolution of a T-long observation (book's factor-2 convention).
key_equations.symbols: f = source frequency; Omega, R = rotation or orbital angular velocity and radius

key_equations.name: Maximum unmodulated observation time
key_equations.meaning: Longest coherent observation before Doppler corrections are needed: about 70 (f/1 kHz)^(-1/2) minutes for Earth's spin and a few hours for its orbit at 1 kHz.

key_equations.name: Angular resolution of a long continuous-wave observation
key_equations.meaning: Diffraction limit lambda/2R of the aperture synthesized by half an orbit around the Sun; about 0.4 arcsec at 1 kHz.

key_equations.name: Number of sky patches
key_equations.meaning: Count of independent demodulations needed for an optimal six-month all-sky search at 1 kHz, before multiplying by spin-down bins.

key_equations.name: Correlation of two detector outputs
key_equations.meaning: Sum of products of simultaneous samples from two detectors.

key_equations.name: Mean correlation
key_equations.meaning: Independent noises and noise-signal cross terms average to zero; only the common background survives.
key_equations.symbols: |h|^2 = mean square background amplitude; N = number of samples

key_equations.name: Variance of the correlation
key_equations.meaning: When the background is much weaker than instrumental noise, the noise-noise product dominates the scatter.

key_equations.name: Stochastic power signal-to-noise ratio
key_equations.meaning: Correlation multiplies the product of the raw per-sample SNRs by the square root of the number of samples.

key_equations.name: Stochastic amplitude signal-to-noise ratio
key_equations.meaning: In amplitude terms the gain is only the fourth root of N: a background 1e4 below the noise needs 1e16 samples; a year at an effective 100 Hz reaches about a factor 100.

key_equations.name: Discrete Fourier transform (Exercise 12.4)
key_equations.meaning: Frequency-domain representation of an M-sample data vector; term-by-term cost of order M^2 versus M ln M for the FFT. The book's printed formula contains a stray factor w_j inside the sum; it is dropped here.
key_equations.symbols: a = frequency index; j = time index

key_equations.name: Correlation theorem (Exercise 12.4)
key_equations.meaning: The transform of the filter output is a simple product, which is why matched filtering is done in the frequency domain with FFTs (and where coloured-noise weighting naturally enters).

key_equations.name: Six-month frequency resolution (Exercise 12.9)
key_equations.meaning: Frequency bin width for a half-year observation, used to count spin-down bins.

key_equations.name: Slowing pulsar clock (Exercise 12.9)
key_equations.meaning: Models spin-down as a pulsar clock running slow relative to barycentric time; resampling removes the linear frequency drift.
key_equations.symbols: t = barycentric time; tau = slowdown time

key_equations.name: Inverse resampling map (Exercise 12.9)
key_equations.meaning: Times at which to resample barycentred data to make a spinning-down signal monochromatic.

key_equations.name: Chirp rate (Exercise 12.10)
key_equations.meaning: Leading-order frequency derivative of a quasi-circular inspiral, used to read the chirp mass off the GW150914 trace.

key_equations.name: Component mass from total and reduced mass (Exercise 12.11)
key_equations.meaning: Larger component mass given total mass M and reduced mass mu (itself fixed by chirp mass and M). Corrected form: the book omits the 1/2 in front of the square root, which would allow m1 > M; the book's Eq. 12.48 follows from the corrected version.

key_equations.name: Sensitivity of component mass to total mass (Exercise 12.11)
key_equations.meaning: At fixed chirp mass, a small error in total mass is amplified enormously in the component masses when they are nearly equal (4 mu/M near 1).

key_equations.name: Hubble-Lemaitre constant from a standard siren
key_equations.meaning: Recession velocity of the host galaxy (redshift corrected for peculiar motion) divided by the gravitational-wave luminosity distance.
key_equations.symbols: D_L = luminosity distance from the chirp amplitude

figures.label: Figure 12.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Whitened strain time series of GW150914 in LIGO Hanford (left) and Livingston (right); the right panel overlays the Hanford trace sign-flipped and shifted by a few milliseconds, the flip reflecting the detectors' relative 90-degree orientation and the shift the source's sky position.
figures.visual_description: Two side-by-side panels titled 'Hanford, Washington (H1)' and 'Livingston, Louisiana (L1)'. Vertical axis 'Strain (10^-21)' from about -1.0 to 1.0; horizontal axis 'Time (s)' from about 0.26 to 0.46. Each trace shows irregular low-amplitude wiggles up to about 0.35 s, then an oscillation whose period shortens and amplitude grows, peaking near 1.0 around 0.41-0.42 s, followed by an abrupt decay to small fluctuations. In the right panel a darker 'L1 observed' curve and a lighter 'H1 observed (shifted, inverted)' curve lie almost on top of each other through the chirp.
figures.what_it_teaches: What a real chirp looks like, that a loud event can be visible by eye, and that two widely separated detectors responding identically (after geometry and light-travel corrections) is strong evidence of an astrophysical origin; the time offset is the only single-baseline localization information.

redesign.idea: Two-detector chirp decoder: a synthetic binary chirp injected into two simulated detector noise streams, with controls to reveal how orientation, sky position and masses shape what each detector records.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the source on a globe (arrival-time offset and relative sign/amplitude update), slides chirp mass (duration and peak frequency change), toggles noise level and a 'flip and shift' button to align the traces, and can play the chirp as audio.

figures.label: Figure 12.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Predicted energy-density spectrum of the stochastic background from binary black hole mergers (shaded bands for different model assumptions), compared with Advanced LIGO's O1 sensitivity and its design sensitivity.
figures.visual_description: Log-log plot: horizontal axis 'Frequency (Hz)' from 10 to 1000; vertical axis Omega_GW from 1e-11 to 1e-6. A solid bowl-shaped curve labelled 'aLIGO O1' at upper left dips to about 1e-7 near 35-40 Hz and rises steeply on both sides. A dotted bowl labelled 'Design' reaches about 1-2e-9 near 20-30 Hz. Two overlapping grey shaded bands (legend 'Flat, Poisson' darker and 'Power, Poisson' lighter) span roughly 1e-10 to 1e-8, rising gently with frequency to a broad maximum at a few hundred Hz and then falling; thin lines 'Flat, Mean' and 'Power, Mean' run through them, and a dark line '3-Delta' rises from about 5e-10 at 10 Hz to about 2e-9 near 300 Hz then plunges near 1 kHz. (Legend names refer to assumed black-hole mass distributions, with Poisson rate uncertainty shaded; this interpretation comes from the source paper, not the book.)
figures.what_it_teaches: The astrophysical background from binary black holes is predicted near Omega_gw of 1e-9, well below the O1 limit but within reach of design sensitivity; backgrounds are compared with detectors in energy-density units rather than strain. (The gently rising low-frequency slope of the bands is the standard inspiral-background shape; the book does not discuss it.)
concepts: energy density parameter of gravitational waves

redesign.idea: Background builder: sum a population of simulated binary mergers across cosmic time into an Omega_gw(f) spectrum and compare it live with sensitivity curves that deepen with observation time.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for merger rate, mass distribution and maximum redshift reshape the predicted band; an observation-time slider lowers the correlation sensitivity bowl as T^(-1/2) in Omega; toggle LIGO pair, 3G pair, LISA and PTA bands.

figures.label: Figure 12.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Geometry for detector response: spherical angles of the incoming direction relative to the detector's zenith and x-arm, and a separate orthonormal basis in the plane of the sky for describing the wave's polarizations.
figures.visual_description: A grey parallelogram 'Detector plane' with edges marked 'x-arm' (toward lower left) and 'y-arm' (toward right). From the corner where the arms meet, unit vectors e_x, e_y and a vertical e_z are drawn. A thin line runs up and right to a hatted N at the top; the polar angle theta is marked between e_z and this line, and a dashed line drops from the far end to the detector plane, where the azimuth phi is marked as an arc from the x-arm. Near the top, a tilted rounded grey rectangle labelled 'Plane of the sky', perpendicular to N, contains two arrows labelled e_x^R and e_y^R.
figures.what_it_teaches: Two frames are needed: detector-fixed angles (theta, phi) feed the antenna factors, while the sky-plane basis defines h+ and hx for all detectors at once.

redesign.idea: 3D response lab: an L-shaped interferometer on a plane, an incoming wave arrow with a sky-plane disk carrying plus/cross ellipses of test particles, and a live readout of F+, Fx and the arm-length difference d:h.
redesign.interaction: Learner orbits the camera, drags the source direction (theta, phi), rotates the sky basis (polarization angle), and chooses pure plus or cross polarization; arms visibly stretch and squeeze, and the four special cases of Exercise 12.3 are one-click presets.

figures.label: Figure 12.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Polarization-averaged antenna power patterns: (a) a single interferometer, largest along the zenith and vanishing in-plane along the arm bisector; (b) the combined pattern of the two LIGO detectors and Virgo viewed from above the North Atlantic, larger but still with weak directions.
figures.visual_description: Two 3D wireframe surfaces in boxed axes. Panel (a), small, at left: a vertically elongated peanut or dumbbell shape extending to plus and minus 1 on the vertical axis and about plus and minus 0.4 horizontally, pinched to a narrow waist at the origin. Panel (b), larger, in a box with axes from -2 to 2: two big, bulbous, overlapping lobes arranged diagonally, one at upper left and one at lower right, joined along a crease, with a small dark dimple where the surfaces meet near the bottom.
figures.what_it_teaches: Interferometers are nearly omnidirectional quadrupolar antennas with blind spots; adding differently oriented detectors fills in sensitivity but does not make it uniform; network geometry matters for localization and polarization.

redesign.idea: Globe of sensitivity: a rotating Earth with placeable detectors (LIGO sites, Virgo, KAGRA, LIGO-India, custom) and the resulting sky map of network sensitivity drawn as a colored celestial sphere or radial surface.
redesign.interaction: Add or remove detectors, change their arm orientations and relative sensitivities, scrub sidereal time; click a sky point to see each detector's F+, Fx and whether a two-detector polarization inversion is well-conditioned (det M near zero warning).

figures.label: Figure 12.5 (LIGO panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: LIGO strain amplitude spectral densities for successive observing runs, measured (O1-O3) and projected (O4, O5), with binary-neutron-star ranges in the legend.
figures.visual_description: Log-log plot titled 'LIGO': vertical axis 'Strain noise [1/sqrt(Hz)]' from 1e-24 to 1e-20; horizontal axis 'Frequency [Hz]' from 10 to a few thousand. Several nested grey curves each fall steeply from the top left below about 20-30 Hz, flatten into a broad bucket between roughly 100 and 500 Hz, and rise gently at high frequency. The upper, measured curves are decorated with many narrow vertical spikes (lines), clustered near 60 Hz harmonics, around 500 Hz and 1 kHz. Legend: O1: 80 Mpc; O2: 100 Mpc; O3: L ~130 Mpc; O3: H ~110 Mpc; O4: 160-190 Mpc; O5: 330 Mpc. The lowest smooth curve (O5) reaches a few times 1e-24.
figures.what_it_teaches: How to read a sensitivity curve: seismic wall, thermal-noise bucket, shot-noise rise, spectral lines; improvements run to run, and how noise level converts into a detection range.
concepts: amplitude spectral density of detector noise

redesign.idea: Noise budget mixer: build the sensitivity curve from separate seismic, thermal, shot/radiation-pressure and line components, then overlay a chirp's characteristic strain to see SNR and range change.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for laser power (shot noise down, radiation pressure up), mirror temperature, suspension isolation and arm length; toggle observing runs; readout of binary-neutron-star range and a sphere whose volume scales as range cubed.

figures.label: Figure 12.5 (Virgo panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Virgo strain amplitude spectral densities for O2 and O3 (measured) and O4, O5 (projected ranges drawn as bands).
figures.visual_description: Log-log plot titled 'Virgo' with the same axes as the LIGO panel (1e-24 to 1e-20 per root Hz; 10 Hz to a few kHz). The O2 and O3 measured curves sit highest, with dense spiky lines, especially at low frequency and around several hundred Hz; below them two thick grey shaded bands (O4 and O5 projections) follow the same bucket shape, the lower reaching near 1e-23 or slightly below in the 100-300 Hz region. Legend: O2: 30 Mpc; O3: 50 Mpc; O4: 90-120 Mpc; O5: 150-260 Mpc.
figures.what_it_teaches: Virgo's lower intrinsic sensitivity relative to LIGO, why the real network pattern differs from the equal-sensitivity picture in Figure 12.4, and that projections carry uncertainty (bands).
concepts: amplitude spectral density of detector noise

redesign.idea: Merge with the LIGO panel into a single network sensitivity explorer where each detector's curve weights its antenna pattern in the sky-sensitivity globe.
redesign.interaction: Select detector and run; network SNR for a chosen source updates as SNRs add in quadrature.

figures.label: Table 12.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Selected event parameters: chirp mass, component masses, final mass, luminosity distance, network SNR, false-alarm rate and 90 percent sky area for six events from 2015-2019, with notes on source-frame masses, why remnant masses are omitted for neutron-star events, and why chirp mass need not equal the value computed from the listed component masses.
figures.visual_description: A shaded table with nine columns: Event name; chirp mass; m1; m2; M_f (solar masses); D_L (Mpc); SNR; FAR (per yr); Omega_sky (sq. deg.). worked_examples.label: Merger frequency of GW150914 and of a binary neutron star (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the highest gravitational-wave frequency reached before merger for GW150914 (chirp mass 30.8 solar masses) and for two 1.4 solar-mass neutron stars, and find the largest chirp mass whose merger lies in LIGO's band.
worked_examples.method: Invert the Chapter 9 phase-to-merger relation for f_gw = omega/pi, normalise to one solar mass (Eq. 12.1), and evaluate at half an orbit remaining, psi = pi (Eq. 12.2). Compare with observation and with neutron-star tidal disruption.
worked_examples.key_insight: Frequency scales inversely with mass, so a detector's low-frequency cutoff is an upper mass limit; point-particle estimates are good to a factor of about two at merger.
worked_examples.result: GW150914: about 130 Hz predicted versus about 250 Hz observed. Neutron stars: a few kHz formally, but the signal weakens near 1 kHz as the stars merge. A 20 Hz cutoff excludes chirp masses above about 200 solar masses.

worked_examples.label: LISA-to-ground handoff time (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: How long after LISA sees a 30 solar-mass chirp-mass binary at 30 mHz will it merge in the ground-based band?
worked_examples.method: Rescale the time-to-merger formula (Eq. 12.3) and substitute the mass and frequency.
worked_examples.key_insight: The steep f^(-8/3) dependence makes months of LISA warning translate into seconds of ground-band signal, enabling advance alerts.

worked_examples.label: Ringdown frequency of the GW150914 remnant (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the ringdown frequency of a black hole of about 68 solar masses (detector frame).
worked_examples.method: Take the dominant quasi-normal angular frequency as about 0.5/M, convert geometrized mass to seconds and divide by 2 pi (Eq. 12.4).
worked_examples.key_insight: A single dimensional estimate lands near the observed peak frequency, supporting a black-hole remnant, even though the ringdown itself was not isolated.

worked_examples.label: Strain from an asymmetric pulsar and required integration (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the continuous-wave amplitude from a neutron star with I = 1e38 kg m^2, spin 60 Hz, distance 1 kpc and asymmetry 1e-6, and how many cycles are needed to detect it with a detector of broadband sensitivity 1e-22.
worked_examples.method: Apply h ~ 2 epsilon Omega^2 I / r (with G/c^4 restored); then require the square-root-of-cycles gain to bridge the ratio of broadband sensitivity to signal amplitude.
worked_examples.key_insight: Tiny amplitudes are reachable only through very long coherent integration, since gain grows as the square root of the cycle count.
worked_examples.result: h about 1e-26; needs about 1e8 cycles, of order a month of data.
concepts: continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars

worked_examples.label: Crab pulsar spin-down fraction (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: If the Crab's gravitational-wave amplitude limit is about 4 percent of its spin-down limit, what fraction of its rotational energy loss can be gravitational?
worked_examples.method: Energy flux scales as amplitude squared; square the amplitude ratio.
worked_examples.key_insight: Amplitude limits tighten quadratically in energy.
worked_examples.result: Roughly (0.04)^2, about 0.16 percent (the book rounds this to below 0.1 percent).

worked_examples.label: Matched filter versus threshold crossing (in-text derivation)
worked_examples.problem: For sampled white Gaussian noise containing a known template of unknown amplitude and arrival time, find the minimum detectable amplitude with and without using the template.
worked_examples.method: Model x_j = n_j + A w_(j-D). Naive: peak must exceed sigma, giving sigma/w_max. Filter: correlate with w; compute mean (A times autocorrelation, peaking at A||w||^2) and variance (sigma^2 ||w||^2) using the white-noise Kronecker delta; set SNR = 1. Specialise to a sinusoid whose squared norm is B^2 N/2.
worked_examples.key_insight: The template's norm integrates over the whole signal, so the threshold drops by the square root of the signal length; long neutron-star chirps gain most.
worked_examples.result: A_min = sigma/||w|| = sigma/[w_max (N/2)^(1/2)]; range grows by N^(1/2), volume by N^(3/2).

worked_examples.label: Does faster sampling help? (in-text argument)
worked_examples.problem: Equation 12.21 seems to promise better sensitivity simply by sampling faster; is that true?
worked_examples.method: Halve the sampling rate: each new sample averages two old ones, so sigma falls by sqrt(2) while N halves, leaving sigma/(N/2)^(1/2) unchanged; push to the extreme of one sample to see the limit; the natural rate is about twice the signal frequency.
worked_examples.key_insight: The gain counts independent pieces of signal, i.e. cycles, not samples.
worked_examples.result: No; the improvement factor is best read as the square root of the number of waveform cycles.

worked_examples.label: Two-detector polarization and inclination (in-text derivation)
worked_examples.problem: With a sky position known from a gamma-ray burst, recover h+ and hx from two detectors and infer the orbital inclination of a binary.
worked_examples.method: Time-shift both streams to a common wave phase; write the responses as a 2x2 linear system with matrix M_12 of antenna factors and invert it. Rotate the sky-plane basis until the recovered polarizations are in quadrature (the edge-on case makes one vanish); then equate their amplitude ratio to (1 + cos^2 iota)/(2 cos iota) from Eq. 9.100 and solve the quadratic (Exercise 12.7).
worked_examples.key_insight: Polarization content is geometric information about the orbit, but near face-on the ratio is quartically flat in iota, so inclination and distance are poorly determined for the loudest systems.
worked_examples.result: Eqs. 12.25-12.26; a 1 percent ratio uncertainty near r = 1 allows iota up to about 30 degrees.

worked_examples.label: False-alarm arithmetic for a year of data (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: How high must a signal-to-noise threshold be so that Gaussian noise produces at most about one false alarm per year (or per two years) in a matched-filter search with many templates?
worked_examples.method: Use the tail bound (with the two-sided factor) for a = 5, 6, 6.5, 8; count raw samples (8 kHz for a year, 2.4e11) and independent filter samples (5 ms period, 6e9); multiply by 1e4 independent templates.
worked_examples.key_insight: Rare-per-sample events are common in big data; thresholds must scale with the number of independent trials, but the Gaussian tail falls so fast that modest increases in a suffice.
worked_examples.result: 5 sigma: probability 6e-7, about 140,000 raw excursions per year; 6 sigma: 2e-9, 12 filter false alarms per year; 6.5 sigma: 8e-11, one per two years; with 1e4 templates, a threshold of about 8 (1.3e-15).

worked_examples.label: Deriving the three-detector null stream (in-text and Exercise 12.8)
worked_examples.problem: Find a linear combination of three detector strains that contains no gravitational-wave signal from a given direction.
worked_examples.method: Solve the first two response equations for h+ and hx (Eq. 12.25), substitute into the third, clear the determinant and rearrange cyclically.
worked_examples.key_insight: Counting unknown waveforms against data streams guarantees N - 2 null combinations; their weights are pairwise antenna determinants.
worked_examples.result: D12 delta3 + D23 delta1 + D31 delta2 = 0; applied to outputs this is the null stream N_123.

worked_examples.label: Doppler coherence time and sky resolution for pulsar searches (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: How long can a 1 kHz continuous signal be observed before Earth's motion must be corrected, and how finely must the sky be gridded for a six-month search?
worked_examples.method: Velocity change Omega^2 R T gives frequency drift f Omega^2 R T/c; set equal to resolution 2/T to get T_max. Treat half an orbit as an aperture of size 2R with diffraction limit lambda/2R; divide 4 pi steradians by the patch size squared.
worked_examples.key_insight: The same Doppler pattern that spoils naive integration is an exquisitely precise direction finder, at the price of an astronomically large search.
worked_examples.result: About 70 minutes (Earth rotation) and a few hours (orbit); about 2e-6 rad (0.4 arcsec) resolution and about 3e12 sky patches.
concepts: angular resolution by orbital aperture synthesis
computational cost of all-sky continuous-wave searches

worked_examples.label: Cross-correlation for a stochastic background (in-text derivation)
worked_examples.problem: Compute the signal-to-noise ratio for detecting a random background common to two co-located, aligned detectors with independent white noise, and estimate what one year of LIGO correlation can reach.
worked_examples.method: Sum products of simultaneous samples: expectation N|h|^2; variance dominated by noise products N sigma1^2 sigma2^2 when the background is weak. Divide and take a square root for amplitude. Use an effective sample rate of about 100 Hz for the LIGO pair.
worked_examples.key_insight: Correlation gains in power as N^(1/2) but in amplitude only as N^(1/4), so a random field far below the noise is much harder to find than a coherent signal of the same amplitude.
worked_examples.result: SNR_amplitude = N^(1/4)|h|/sqrt(sigma1 sigma2); 1e4 below noise needs 1e16 samples (about 100,000 years at kHz rates); a year at 100 Hz (3e9 samples) reaches about 100 below broadband noise, 1e4 lower in energy.

worked_examples.label: Standard-siren Hubble constant from GW170817 (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Measure H0 from a neutron-star merger whose host galaxy is identified.
worked_examples.method: Obtain the luminosity distance from the gravitational-wave amplitude and inclination posterior, the recession velocity from the host redshift corrected for peculiar motion, and form their ratio as a posterior distribution; later add a radio constraint on the jet viewing angle.
worked_examples.key_insight: Inclination uncertainty for nearly face-on systems dominates the error; an electromagnetic jet-angle measurement sharply narrows it.
worked_examples.result: A broad posterior peaking near 70 km/s/Mpc between Planck and SH0ES; with radio jet constraints, 70.3 plus or minus 5 km/s/Mpc.

worked_examples.label: Detection-rate growth from sensitivity (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Why did detections jump from 3 in O1 to 8 in O2 to 39 in half of O3?
worked_examples.method: Amplitude sensitivity improvement by a factor k extends range by k and volume (rate) by k^3; add better glitch rejection with three detectors and a lower significance threshold.
worked_examples.key_insight: Cubic volume scaling makes modest noise improvements pay off dramatically.
worked_examples.result: A factor 2 in noise gives 8 times the rate.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A coherent detector network is like aperture synthesis in radio interferometry: separated detectors combined with correct phases act as one larger instrument.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Cited (after Finn) to explain why combining data before thresholding is more powerful than coincidence and how directional information emerges.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gravitational-wave wavelengths are comparable to or larger than Earth, so the network gains localization mainly from timing and antenna patterns rather than true imaging.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side radio array and GW network: moving detectors apart sharpens a sky-localization ellipse just as baseline length sharpens a radio beam.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Earth's orbit as a synthesized telescope aperture for a continuous gravitational wave.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: angular resolution by orbital aperture synthesis
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Turns the direction-dependent Doppler modulation into a diffraction-limit estimate lambda/2R and a count of sky patches.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only works for signals coherent over months and assumes perfect phase models including spin-down.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Animate a detector circling the Sun while a wavefront sweeps past; show phase residuals for a slightly wrong sky position growing through the year.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The cosmological gravitational-wave background is the gravitational counterpart of the cosmic microwave background, but from a far earlier epoch because gravity has never been obscured.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates why a relic background would be scientifically priceless and why its present intensity is so uncertain.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Unlike the CMB it is not thermal, need not be detectable with any planned instrument, and is likely masked by astrophysical backgrounds.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Timeline of the Universe with a 'last scattering' wall for photons and none for gravitons, letting the learner see which epoch each background reveals.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The square-root-of-N matched-filter gain is the same random-walk scaling that governs averaging repeated measurements.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reassures the reader that a result derived for a sinusoid is general.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Holds for stationary Gaussian noise and a perfectly known template; mismatched templates and coloured noise reduce the gain.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Random-walk plot of accumulated noise versus linearly accumulated signal, with the crossing point marking detection.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Building LIGO required theory-experiment partnership like building large particle accelerators, where theory both justifies the cost and enables recognition of new phenomena.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why source modelling preceded and shaped detection.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Each pulsar in a timing array is like a separate gravitational-wave detector whose noise is independent, so correlating pulsars mirrors correlating interferometers.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Links nHz background searches to the cross-correlation method just derived.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Pulsar-Earth baselines give a specific angular correlation pattern (Hellings-Downs) not discussed; data are irregularly sampled times of arrival, not strain.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Sky map of pulsars with pairwise correlation plotted against angular separation as a simulated background is switched on.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A neutron star is essentially one enormous atomic nucleus, so flinging off part of it is like breaking a nucleus into ever smaller pieces.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a vivid picture of how merger ejecta become heavy elements.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Misleading as nuclear physics: heavy elements form mainly by rapid neutron capture on seed nuclei in decompressed ejecta, with fission only recycling the heaviest; a neutron star is gravitationally, not strongly, bound.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Nuclide-chart animation of neutron capture racing along the neutron-rich side, then beta decays to stability, to replace the fission picture.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The detector response as a double contraction d:h, in the spirit of Schutz's tensors as machines that eat vectors or tensors and return numbers.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Makes the complicated angular dependence of interferometer response a single frame-free operation.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Valid in the long-wavelength limit (arm length much shorter than wavelength), not for LISA at high frequencies.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Visual 'machine' with two input slots (detector tensor, wave tensor) and a strain output dial, with components lighting up as they contribute.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: LISA as an early-warning system for ground-based detectors and telescopes.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Communicates the practical payoff of seeing the same binary months before merger.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Requires sources close enough to be above LISA's noise; rates are uncertain.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Frequency-time track of a binary crossing from the LISA band to the LIGO band with a countdown clock.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravitational-wave detectors can be pointed at a source like telescopes.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Waves cannot be focused because they barely interact with matter; interferometers are nearly omnidirectional with broad quadrupolar patterns, and localization comes from networks.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Other astronomy is done with aimed instruments.
concepts: complementarity of gravitational and electromagnetic observations

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every gravitational-wave event should have an electromagnetic counterpart, and EM surveys tell us which GW sources exist.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Binary black holes in vacuum emit essentially no light, and GW sources are selected by mass and compactness, not luminosity; counterparts are prized exceptions.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A signal must stand visibly above the noise to be detected.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Matched filtering detects known waveforms far below the raw noise; GW170817 never exceeded 1e-22 in strain yet is the highest-SNR event of its time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: GW150914's trace was visible by eye, and intuition equates detection with seeing.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Sampling data faster improves matched-filter sensitivity because N grows.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Noise per sample changes in step with N, leaving the threshold unchanged; the gain counts signal cycles.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A 5 sigma excursion is so rare it must be real.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In a year of kHz data with many templates, 5 sigma noise excursions occur hundreds of thousands of times; thresholds near 8 are needed, and glitches push them higher.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: 5 sigma is the particle-physics discovery standard.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A stochastic background 1e4 times below the noise is as detectable as a pulsar 1e4 times below the noise.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coherent signals gain as the square root of time in amplitude, random backgrounds only as the fourth root; the background would need about 100,000 years of correlation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are 'long integrations of a weak signal'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If the chirp mass is known to 0.1 percent and the total mass well, the component masses are also precise.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Near equal masses the mapping from (chirp mass, total mass) to (m1, m2) is extremely sensitive, so small total-mass errors become large component errors (Exercise 12.11).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Two equations in two unknowns seem to fix the answer cleanly.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The loudest (face-on) binaries give the best distance measurements.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Face-on amplitudes are insensitive to inclination at second order, so distance is degenerate with inclination; moderately inclined systems like GW190814 constrain distance better.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Higher SNR normally means smaller errors.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Two detectors can locate a source on the sky.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: One time delay only restricts the source to a ring; at least three detectors (two independent delays), antenna-pattern amplitudes, or an EM counterpart are needed.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Two ears localize sound (but using head shadowing and spectral cues).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A detector that barely responds to an event contributes nothing.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Virgo's weak response to GW170817 showed the source lay near its antenna-pattern null, sharply reducing the sky area.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Information seems tied to signal strength.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: GW170814's polarization test ruled out alternative theories of gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It only disfavoured pure scalar or pure vector polarization, which no viable theory predicts; realistic alternatives add extra modes that the data could not test.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Headline results sound more sweeping than they are.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Black-hole mergers can never produce light.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In a gas-rich environment (such as an AGN disk) a recoiling remnant could shock the gas and produce a flare, as proposed for GW190521.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Black holes are black and binary black holes in vacuum are dark.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Detector noise is white, so the simple matched filter derived in the text is what LIGO uses.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Noise is strongly frequency dependent; real searches weight the correlation by the inverse noise spectrum in the frequency domain.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The derivation assumes white noise for clarity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian (gravity-gradient) noise can be removed with better vibration isolation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It acts through gravity on the test masses exactly as a wave does and cannot be shielded, only reduced by moving underground or to space.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Seismic noise is handled by isolation, and the two share a source.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Most heavy elements such as gold and uranium come from ordinary supernovae.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: GW170817's kilonova supports compact mergers as a major r-process site.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Older textbooks attribute all heavy elements to supernovae.
concepts: r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The LIGO signals directly prove that the merging objects have event horizons.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The black-hole label rests on the measured masses and the extreme compactness implied by the orbital frequency reached, which no conventional object could have; a direct test would require resolving the remnant's quasi-normal mode spectrum, which LIGO-Virgo did not claim for GW150914.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular accounts present the detection as 'seeing' black holes.

thought_experiments.name: Point particles with half an orbit left
thought_experiments.setup: Follow a point-mass inspiral whose frequency formally diverges and ask at what frequency meaningful power stops.
thought_experiments.lesson: Cutting at orbital phase pi gives a usable merger-frequency scale inversely proportional to chirp mass and an upper mass limit for any detector band.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated spiral with a phase-remaining counter and frequency readout that stops at psi = pi, with the learner dragging the mass slider.

thought_experiments.name: Halving the sampling rate
thought_experiments.setup: Resample a data stream at half the rate, averaging adjacent samples, and recompute the matched-filter threshold.
thought_experiments.lesson: The threshold is invariant; sensitivity depends on cycles of signal, not bookkeeping of samples.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Toggle sample rates on a noisy sinusoid while an SNR meter stays constant until the rate drops below twice the signal frequency.

thought_experiments.name: Rotate the sky basis until the polarizations are in quadrature
thought_experiments.setup: Reconstruct h+ and hx from two detectors in an arbitrary sky basis, then rotate the basis; start with an edge-on binary where one component can be made to vanish.
thought_experiments.lesson: The orbit's projected orientation and inclination are encoded in the polarization ellipse; the right basis exposes them.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Polarization-ellipse dial: rotating the basis mixes two sinusoids until they become 90 degrees out of phase; the ellipse's axis ratio gives iota.

thought_experiments.name: Wrong direction leaks signal into the null stream
thought_experiments.setup: Build a null stream for an assumed sky position when a real signal comes from elsewhere.
thought_experiments.lesson: Residual signal power in the null stream is a direction finder: the true direction nulls the signal.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Sky heat map of null-stream power updating as the learner drags a trial direction; a dark spot appears at the true source.

thought_experiments.name: Time slides
thought_experiments.setup: Shift one detector's data by more than the light-travel time and rerun the coincidence search many times.
thought_experiments.lesson: All coincidences found must be accidental, so their rate calibrates the background of real searches including glitches.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Two glitchy data strips with a draggable offset; count accidental coincidences per slide and build a background histogram.

thought_experiments.name: Two co-located, aligned detectors
thought_experiments.setup: Place two identical detectors at the same spot so they see identical background strain but independent instrumental noise, and multiply their outputs.
thought_experiments.lesson: The common random signal survives averaging while independent noise cancels, with SNR growing as N^(1/2) in power and N^(1/4) in amplitude.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Two noisy traces sharing a faint hidden common component; a running product-sum crawls upward out of a widening noise band.

thought_experiments.name: GW170817 at 150 Mpc
thought_experiments.setup: Move the observed event to a more typical distance.
thought_experiments.lesson: The gamma-ray burst would have gone undetected, localization would have ballooned and a days-long kilonova would likely have been missed: the first multimessenger event was lucky.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Distance slider showing SNR, sky-area ellipse and number of candidate galaxies growing, with a fading kilonova light curve.

historical_notes.event: Built the first resonant-bar gravitational-wave detectors, aiming to catch supernovae.
historical_notes.significance: Began experimental gravitational-wave research and set the supernova burst as an early target.

historical_notes.event: Nobel Prize for pioneering X-ray astronomy, including the discovery of X-ray binaries first seen with sounding rockets in the 1960s.
historical_notes.significance: X-ray binaries showed compact objects can survive in binaries after the first supernova.

historical_notes.event: Discovery of the binary pulsar, the first double neutron star system.
historical_notes.significance: Started decades of work on neutron-star binary formation and provided evidence of systems surviving two supernovae.

historical_notes.event: Accidental discovery of the cosmic microwave background at Bell Labs (Nobel Prize 1978).
historical_notes.significance: Offered as the electromagnetic analogue of a cosmological gravitational-wave background.

historical_notes.event: First mention of matched filtering, a radar technique, for gravitational-wave (bar detector) data analysis.
historical_notes.significance: The method that makes weak binary signals detectable.

historical_notes.event: Coherent network analysis and the null stream were introduced (Gursel and Tinto 1989), systematized (Bose et al.; Finn 2001, with the aperture-synthesis analogy) and promoted for localization and vetoes (Wen and Schutz 2005).
historical_notes.significance: The foundation of multi-detector analysis used for glitch rejection and sky localization.

historical_notes.event: GW150914 recorded on 14 September 2015 during an engineering run, first seen by collaboration members at the Albert Einstein Institute in Hanover, announced on 11 February 2016.
historical_notes.significance: First direct detection of gravitational waves and first observation of a binary black hole, a century after general relativity.

historical_notes.event: GW170817 detected by three detectors, gamma-ray burst 1.7 s later, kilonova found in NGC 4993 about 11 hours later by six teams; about 70 observatories followed.
historical_notes.significance: Birth of gravitational-wave multimessenger astronomy, confirming merger origins of short bursts and kilonovae and giving the first standard-siren H0.

historical_notes.event: Proposals that neutron star-black hole (1974) and neutron star-neutron star (1989) mergers eject neutron-rich matter producing heavy elements and are linked to gamma-ray bursts.
Proposed measuring H0 from gravitational-wave distances by statistically combining redshifts of all galaxies in a localization volume.
historical_notes.significance: Method applied to GW190814 without an identified host.

historical_notes.event: Gamma-ray bursts discovered by satellites monitoring nuclear test bans.
historical_notes.significance: Start of the path to the short-burst/merger connection.

historical_notes.event: Neutrinos from supernova SN1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud were detected.
historical_notes.significance: Cited as proof that particles can reach us directly from a collapsing core; the book argues gravitational waves are the only other such probe and that neutrino timing would anchor a Galactic supernova search.

historical_notes.event: Pointed out that stellar-mass black-hole binaries like the LIGO sources could be seen first by LISA and then, months later, merge in the ground-based band.
historical_notes.significance: The origin of the multiband early-warning idea the book quantifies with Eq. 12.3.

historical_notes.event: Before O1, predictions favoured about one detection per year at design sensitivity, most likely a neutron-star binary near 100 Mpc; O1 began two to three times less sensitive than design.
historical_notes.significance: Explains why a strong binary black hole signal during the engineering run came as a double surprise.

applications_and_observations.topic: LISA Galactic white-dwarf binaries and confusion noise
applications_and_observations.details: Many thousands of non-evolving Galactic binaries, mostly white dwarfs, will be individually detected; below about 1 mHz their overlap forms confusion noise exceeding LISA's instrumental noise.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Confusion dominates below ~1 mHz (text also quotes 0.1 mHz for background dominance)

applications_and_observations.details: At tens of nHz the first expected signal is a background from 1e8-1e9 solar-mass binaries, possibly with resolvable individual systems.

applications_and_observations.topic: Binary neutron star in the ground band
applications_and_observations.details: Two 1.4 solar-mass stars (chirp mass 1.2) would formally merge near 4 kHz, but hydrodynamic merger weakens the signal near 1 kHz; the signal lasts about 2.5 minutes from 20 Hz (Exercise 12.2).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ~4 kHz formal; ~1 kHz actual; ~150 s from 20 Hz

applications_and_observations.details: Mergers of 1e4-1e7 solar-mass black holes, visible across the Universe back to the first galaxies, tracing galaxy mergers; an equal-mass 1e6 pair spends of order a month in band from 0.1 mHz.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: LISA band 0.1-100 mHz; ~1 month from 0.1 mHz (Exercise 12.2e quotes 26 days; our own estimate with Eq. 12.3 gives ~40 days)

applications_and_observations.details: Stellar black holes of 10-50 solar masses captured by 1e6 solar-mass holes enter the LISA band with 1e5-1e6 orbits remaining; tens per year to 100 Mpc or beyond, enabling strong-field tests including spin-orbit precession.

No detections by mid-2021. All-sky searches 20 Hz-2 kHz limit ellipticity to about 1e-7 in places and amplitude to about 1e-25; targeted searches: Crab amplitude below 1e-25, ellipticity a few times 1e-5, about 4 percent of spin-down limit; some pulsars reach a few 1e-26 and 1e-7. Sco X-1 searches also null.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: epsilon < 1e-7; h < 1e-25; Crab h < 1e-25, 4% of spin-down

applications_and_observations.details: O1 limit Omega_gw < 1.7e-7; Advanced LIGO design reaches about 1e-9, where the binary black hole background is predicted; LISA could reach about 1e-10; cosmological predictions span 1e-15 to above 1e-8, likely beyond even third-generation detectors; best probe may be CMB polarization.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 1.7e-7 (O1); ~1e-9 (design); ~1e-10 (LISA); LIGO pair correlated below ~100 Hz (10 ms light-travel separation)

applications_and_observations.topic: Interferometer noise sources and design trade-offs
applications_and_observations.details: Shot noise (high f), thermal noise (mid band), seismic noise (low f), suspension resonance lines, mains lines at 60 Hz (LIGO) and 50 Hz (Virgo); higher laser power reduces shot noise but heats mirrors and adds radiation pressure; KAGRA's cryogenic mirrors limit usable power; Newtonian noise motivates underground KAGRA and Einstein Telescope, and space-based LISA below 1 Hz.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Sampling 8 or 16 kHz; LIGO band minimum ~20 Hz

applications_and_observations.topic: Computing cost of an optimal all-sky pulsar search (Exercise 12.9)
applications_and_observations.details: Six months of 4 kHz data (6e10 samples), about 1e12-3e12 sky patches, a very large number of spin-down values, FFT per combination; the book's estimate totals about 5e35 floating-point operations, 3e28 flops to keep pace, versus 4e17 flops for the fastest 2021 supercomputer.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 5e35 operations; ~1e11 supercomputers (the exercise's spin-down count appears overstated; see gaps)

applications_and_observations.details: Binary black hole seen by both LIGO detectors; peak strain about 1e-21; chirp mass 30.8 (detector frame) or 28 (source frame); components 36 and 29, remnant 62 solar masses; 410 Mpc; SNR 24; 600 sq. deg.; graviton mass below 1.2e-22 eV; heavier than any known stellar black hole (previous maximum about 20).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: SNR 24; FAR 5e-6/yr; D_L 410 Mpc; m_graviton < 1.2e-22 eV

applications_and_observations.details: GW151012 and GW151226 with chirp masses 15.2 and 8.9 solar masses, closer to X-ray binary black-hole masses.

First three-detector detection; sky area 87 sq. deg., 15 percent of GW150914's; pure tensor polarization favoured over pure scalar (Bayes factor ~1000) and pure vector (~200). O2 also had GW170729 at 2.8 Gpc.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 87 sq. deg.; Bayes factors 1000, 200; D_L 600 Mpc

applications_and_observations.details: About 100 s in band; merger 12:41:04.4 UTC on 17 August 2017; GRB170817A 1.7 s later; Livingston glitch gated out; Virgo's weak response localized the source to ~31 sq. deg.; distance 40 plus or minus 8 Mpc; fewer than 100 galaxies in the volume; kilonova in NGC 4993 after ~11 hours; ~70 observatories; SNR 32; masses 1.44 and 1.28; tidal limits exclude very stiff equations of state; jet viewing angle 14-28 degrees; about 10 percent of professional astronomers took part.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: SNR 32; 40 Mpc; 1.7 s delay; 31 sq. deg. (16 final); H0 = 70.3 plus or minus 5 km/s/Mpc with jet constraint

applications_and_observations.details: Spectra of the GW170817 ejecta support mergers as the main source of r-process elements; decays of uranium-238 and thorium-232 help heat Earth's interior, driving plate tectonics and sustaining the molten core and magnetic field.
Expected nearest binary neutron star merger in a year is about 100 Mpc; 40 Mpc lies in the nearest ~7 percent of that volume ((0.4)^3 about 6 percent).
Total mass ~3.4 solar masses, heavier than known double neutron stars; significance from Livingston alone; 8284 sq. deg.; ~150-160 Mpc; no counterpart.

Total ~150 solar masses, 85 plus 65, remnant 142 (an intermediate-mass black hole); four cycles over 0.1 s; SNR 14.7; possible AGN flare starting 34 days and peaking 50 days after merger, with a predicted repeat in ~2 years; higher multipoles moved distance from 4.1 to 5.3 Gpc.

23 plus 2.6 solar masses, mass ratio ~9:1, companion in the 2.2-6 solar-mass gap; inclination near 45 degrees and higher harmonics gave a good distance (241 Mpc) and a statistical H0 of 70 km/s/Mpc when combined with GW170817.

O1: 3 events; O2: 8 events in about 9 months with Virgo in the last month; O3a (GWTC-2): 39 events in 5 months with a false-alarm threshold of 2 per year (about one expected false positive). Planned A+ upgrades (factor 3-4) and LIGO-India could give a dozen events per day by the mid-2020s according to the book.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Formulas use G = c = 1 and are rescaled by 1 solar mass (about 4.93e-6 s) and a benchmark frequency to give numerical coefficients (8.0 kHz, 4.0 kHz, 2.9 s, 16 kHz).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Eq. 12.5 must have G/c^4 restored for SI inputs.

notation_and_conventions.convention: For inspirals f_gw = omega/pi with omega the orbital angular frequency (twice the orbital frequency); for ringdown f = omega/2 pi with omega the mode angular frequency.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Two different omegas in adjacent pages.

notation_and_conventions.convention: epsilon = m2/m1 with m1 the larger mass, stated range 0 < epsilon <= 0.5.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Probably intended <= 1; conflicts with other uses of epsilon (neutron-star asymmetry in Eq. 12.5; r - 1 in Exercise 12.7).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Detector frame: arms along e_x and e_y, zenith e_z; source direction (theta, phi) measured from zenith and x-arm. Wave frame: z along propagation direction N, sky-plane basis e_x^R, e_y^R defining h+ and hx.
A : B := A^{jk} B_{jk}, full contraction of two rank-2 spatial tensors.
Delta_int = arm-length difference (displacement); delta_int = Delta_int/L = dimensionless strain; delta_a for detector a.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Delta_ab is not a Kronecker delta; D_ab are determinants.

notation_and_conventions.convention: x_j data samples (M of them), w_j template samples (N nonzero), n_j noise with standard deviation sigma, Delta t sampling interval, D arrival index, ||w||^2 = sum of w_j^2, angle brackets = expectation, var = variance, (x*w)_k = sum_j x_j w_(j-k).
notation_and_conventions.notes: M is also mass and the response matrix; N is also the null stream label and samples count in the correlation section; the operation called convolution is a correlation.

notation_and_conventions.convention: |h|^2 denotes the mean square amplitude <h^2> of a random background; sigma_1, sigma_2 are per-sample instrumental noise standard deviations.
The book takes the frequency resolution of an observation of length T as 2/T.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Most signal-processing texts use 1/T for bin width; factors of two in the Doppler and spin-down estimates follow from this choice.

notation_and_conventions.convention: T denotes a common reference time at which the same wave phase passes each detector (or the geocentre or barycentre).
notation_and_conventions.notes: T also denotes signal duration, observation length and, in Exercise 12.9, the pulsar clock.

notation_and_conventions.convention: iota is the angle between the orbital angular momentum and the line of sight (0 face-on, 90 degrees edge-on).
notation_and_conventions.notes: In Exercise 12.4 the same Greek iota glyph is used for the imaginary unit.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Events are named GWyymmdd; all times are in UTC.

Table 12.1 lists source-frame masses (corrected with Eq. 9.163), luminosity distance D_L, network matched-filter SNR, false-alarm rate FAR per year, and 90 percent sky area Omega_sky in square degrees; M_f is the remnant mass.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Omega_sky is unrelated to Omega_gw or the spin angular velocity Omega.

notation_and_conventions.convention: O1, O2, O3 (O3a/O3b), O4, O5 denote successive LIGO-Virgo observing runs; A+ is the planned LIGO upgrade; 3G denotes third-generation ground detectors.

difficulty.notes: The astrophysics survey (12.2) and detection stories (12.4) are accessible to anyone who has read Chapter 9. Section 12.3 needs comfort with probability, variances of sums, 2x2 linear algebra and some Fourier ideas; the discrete-sample treatment keeps it elementary but several printed equations contain slips that can confuse careful readers. Conceptually the hardest ideas are the difference between coherent and stochastic integration, trials factors, and the null stream. Very little differential geometry is required.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive the matched-filter gain from a sampled sinusoid in white noise: the threshold goes from sigma/w_max to sigma/[w_max sqrt(N/2)], then argue via resampling that N really counts cycles.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A two-line calculation delivers the central idea of modern GW data analysis, and the resampling twist prevents the most common misreading.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Noisy data strip with a hidden sinusoidal chirp; learner slides a template across it and watches the correlation peak rise out of the noise as signal length grows, with a sample-rate toggle that leaves SNR unchanged.

teaching_gems.gem: Turn false-alarm probabilities into counts using real sampling rates, run lengths and template numbers (140,000 five-sigma excursions per year).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts abstract tail probabilities into a visceral sense of why thresholds near SNR 8 are required.
teaching_gems.app_idea: False-alarm calculator with sliders for threshold a, sample rate, duration and number of templates, plotting expected false alarms on a log scale with a Gaussian tail shading.

teaching_gems.gem: Count unknowns against data streams: two polarizations need two detectors; a third gives direction plus redundancy; each further detector adds a null stream.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Structural insight before algebra, and it generalizes immediately to any network.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Network builder where adding detectors updates a counter of 'unknowns solved' and 'null streams available', with a demo glitch that shows up only in the null stream.

teaching_gems.gem: Write detector response as the double contraction of a detector tensor with the wave tensor, then check special directions.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Leverages the book's tensor-as-machine picture to tame messy angular formulas and makes network analysis frame-independent.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 3D interferometer with test-mass arms responding to a user-oriented plus/cross wave, showing the contraction numerically component by component.

teaching_gems.gem: Contrast coherent and random integration: a pulsar 1e4 below the noise is routine, a background 1e4 below the noise needs 100,000 years.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single startling comparison makes N^(1/2) versus N^(1/4) unforgettable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Race between two integrators on the same noise: one matched filter, one cross-correlator, with a time axis in years and a finish line at SNR 5.

teaching_gems.gem: Treat the Doppler modulation of continuous waves as both curse and blessing: it breaks naive integration after about an hour, but makes Earth's orbit a telescope with sub-arcsecond resolution, which in turn explodes the search cost.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Chains three consequences of one physical effect into a coherent story about why pulsar searches are computationally limited.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Orbiting detector and a sky grid that refines as observation time grows, with a counter of templates and a computing-time gauge compared against a supercomputer.

teaching_gems.gem: Estimate merger frequency by stopping a point-particle inspiral at half an orbit, then confront the estimate with GW150914 and neutron stars.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows how far a crude but principled cut-off gets you and why the detector band acts as a mass filter.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Mass slider moving a binary's chirp track across overlaid PTA, LISA and LIGO sensitivity bands, marking f_final and time in band.

teaching_gems.gem: Explain that face-on binaries are loudest yet measure distance worst because the amplitude ratio is flat (iota^4/8) near face-on.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A counterintuitive, quantitative result that directly explains the broad GW170817 H0 posterior.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot of |h+|/|hx| versus inclination with a 1 percent error band showing the allowed inclination range, linked to a distance-error bar and an H0 posterior.

teaching_gems.gem: Use Virgo's near-silence during GW170817 as information: a null in one antenna pattern localizes the source.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Memorable real story that teaches antenna patterns and Bayesian reasoning about non-detections.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Sky map where the learner sees LIGO-only localization band, then adds Virgo's weak signal to carve it down to the true patch.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The sensitivity scalings are printed with the wrong sign of the exponent: h_min proportional to T^(1/2) for continuous waves and T^(1/4) for stochastic backgrounds, although the text says sensitivity improves with time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may think detectable amplitude grows with observation time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State h_min proportional to T^(-1/2) and T^(-1/4) explicitly and show both as falling lines on a log plot.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Matched-filter derivation slips: Eq. 12.15 carries a spurious factor A in the middle expression; the text says the autocorrelation vanishes for |k - D| >= M (should be the template length N); Eq. 12.18 omits the template weights; Eq. 12.19 gives var = sigma^2 (w*w)_(k-D), whereas for white noise the variance is sigma^2 ||w||^2 at every lag (the two agree only at k = D, so Eq. 12.20 is still right); the 'integral' is a sum.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Careful readers trying to reproduce the derivation get stuck or conclude the noise vanishes away from the peak.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the corrected chain (mean A(w*w)_(k-D), variance sigma^2||w||^2, SNR A||w||/sigma) and animate that noise level is constant across lags while the mean peaks.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Normalization of the detector response: with d = L(e_x e_x - e_y e_y) and e+ = e^R_x e^R_x - e^R_y e^R_y, a wave from the zenith gives d:h = 2 L h+, whereas the physical difference of arm-length changes is L h+ (each arm changes by hL/2). The book's Eq. 12.9 therefore overstates the displacement by a factor 2 and its F+, Fx are twice the conventional antenna functions (our check).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners comparing with standard antenna-pattern formulas (maximum 1) or computing absolute arm displacements get a factor 2 discrepancy.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use D = (1/2)(e_x e_x - e_y e_y) for the dimensionless detector tensor, or say explicitly that only ratios are used; Exercise 12.3's relative results are unaffected.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eq. 12.29's bounds omit the factor 2 from the two-sided probability in Eq. 12.27, yet the numbers quoted (6e-7 at 5 sigma, etc.) include it; Exercise 12.5(a) writes exp(-z^2/2) on the right side where exp(-a^2/2) is meant.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Computed false-alarm probabilities come out a factor of two smaller than the text's.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write 2 phi(a)/a and flag one-sided versus two-sided tails explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 12.11's Eq. 12.47 is missing a factor 1/2 in front of the square root (m1/M = 1/2 + (1/2)(1 - 4 mu/M)^(1/2)); Eq. 12.48 is consistent with the corrected form. Eq. 12.41's Fourier transform contains a stray factor w_j, and it asks for the transform of w while defining that of x.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students cannot verify the stated derivative or obtain m1 <= M.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use corrected forms in any app or tutor derivation; check limiting cases (equal masses give m1 = M/2).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 12.9's spin-down parametrization is dimensionally inconsistent: with t_p = t(1 - t/tau), df/dt = -2 f0/tau (not -2/tau), and a 2 kHz pulsar halving in 1000 years gives 1/tau of about 8e-12 per second, not 8e-8 s^-2; the number of spin-down bins (4e10) and final totals then look overstated by about 1e4 by our own check. Exercise 12.7(g) quotes a 7 percent change in 1 + cos^2 iota for iota between 0 and 0.53 rad, whereas it changes by about 13 percent (7 percent is the change in 1 + cos iota).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students following the steps get different numbers and lose confidence.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Rework the estimates consistently; the qualitative conclusion (optimal all-sky search far out of reach) survives, since even 5e31 operations is hopeless.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Numerical mismatches in the source survey: for two 1.4 solar-mass neutron stars Eq. 12.1 gives 1 kHz at about 23 rad of orbital phase (roughly 3.7 orbits), not the 1.6 orbits stated; the same equation gives about 3.3 kHz at merger rather than 4 kHz; Exercise 12.2(e) claims 26 days where Eq. 12.3 gives about 40 days for an equal-mass 1e6 solar-mass pair from 0.1 mHz (our estimates); the stated mass-ratio range 0 < m2/m1 <= 0.5 excludes equal masses.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Plug-in checks disagree with the text.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Recompute in the app from the formulas and present book numbers as rounded order-of-magnitude values.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Table 12.1 lists GW190521's distance as 5.3 in a column labelled Mpc (it is 5.3 Gpc); masses in the table are source-frame (GW150914 chirp mass 28) while the text uses the detector-frame 30.8; GW170817's sky area is 16 sq. deg. in the table versus 31 in the text (initial versus final analyses).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Apparent contradictions between table and prose.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label frames and analysis versions explicitly in any data display.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Historical details inconsistent or misprinted: 12.4 says LIGO was preparing on '15 September' with local times 03:50 (Livingston) and 01:50 (Hanford), whereas GW150914 occurred on 14 September 2015 at 09:50:45 UTC (04:50 CDT, 02:50 PDT, 11:50 CEST in Hanover); Virgo is said to have joined O2 on 1 August 2016 (it was 2017); O1 is described as spanning 16 months (it ran about four months, Sept 2015 to Jan 2016).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners quoting the book will propagate wrong dates.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Heuristics that are physically loose: the shot-noise f^(1/2) rise is derived from photons per sample, while real interferometer shot noise in strain rises roughly linearly above the arm-cavity pole; the r-process is described as fission of neutron-star chunks rather than rapid neutron capture; F+ and Fx are said to depend only on theta and phi though they also depend on the polarization angle.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Plausible but incorrect mental models that later courses must undo.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Tutor should present these as cartoons and give the standard mechanism (cavity response; neutron capture and beta decay; three-angle antenna functions).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Coloured noise and the noise-weighted inner product are essentially skipped: the derivation assumes white noise, and the frequency-domain treatment appears only as an FFT efficiency exercise.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot connect the toy filter to the sensitivity curves or to the standard SNR integral over |h(f)|^2/S_h(f).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a bridge: whitening the data by the ASD turns coloured noise into white noise, recovering the toy result; show the integrand 4|h(f)|^2/S_h(f) on Figure 12.5.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symbol overloading: epsilon (mass ratio, neutron-star asymmetry, r - 1), M (chirp mass script M, total mass, data length, response matrix), N (samples, template length, null stream), T (duration, common time, pulsar clock), Omega (spin rate, Omega_gw, Omega_sky), iota (inclination, imaginary unit).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Easy to misapply formulas across subsections.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use distinct symbols in app materials (q for mass ratio, epsilon for ellipticity, N_s for samples).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Time-sensitive content is out of date relative to 2026: pulsar timing arrays reported evidence for a nHz background in 2023; GWTC-3 and O4 catalogs contain far more events (including further mass-gap and very massive systems); ESA adopted LISA in 2024 for a launch in the mid-2030s; the 'dozen events per day by mid-decade' projection has not materialised.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may treat mid-2021 limits and plans as current.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair each 'as of mid-2021' statement with a live data panel or an update note maintained by the course.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Crab spin-down statement (4 percent amplitude implies less than 0.1 percent of energy) is slightly off: 0.04 squared is 0.16 percent. The text also calls a cross-correlation a 'convolution' throughout.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor confusion when checking numbers or reading signal-processing references.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Quote about 0.2 percent; name the operation correlation and note the relation to convolution.

tutor_notes: Open with a question: 'If gravitational waves stretch LIGO's arms by less than a proton's width, how can anyone be sure a wiggle is real?' Use it to motivate the chapter's three pillars: predicted waveforms, statistics of noise, and multiple detectors.
Before 12.3, check that the learner can state what h+ and hx are and how a ring of test particles responds; the detector-tensor formalism collapses without this.

Teach matched filtering in this order: data model, naive threshold, correlation with template, mean and (correctly) constant variance, SNR = A||w||/sigma, sinusoid gives sqrt(N/2), then the resampling argument converting samples to cycles. Only then mention coloured noise and whitening.
Check understanding with: 'Doubling the observation of a pulsar improves amplitude sensitivity by what factor? And for a stochastic background?' (sqrt 2 versus 2^(1/4)).

When discussing significance, have the learner compute expected false alarms for their own choice of threshold, sample rate and template count before revealing why SNR about 8 is used; then introduce glitches to show why even that is not enough for one detector.
Use the counting argument (two unknown waveforms) before deriving the null stream; ask how many null streams a five-detector network has (three).
Common learner question: 'Why not just point more detectors at the source?' Answer with the unfocusable, all-sky nature of interferometers and antenna patterns (Figure 12.4).
Common learner question: 'If the chirp mass is so precise, why are component masses fuzzy?' Walk through Exercise 12.11's sensitivity blow-up near equal masses (using the corrected Eq. 12.47).

Common learner question: 'Why was GW170817 the most significant event if it was so weak?' Because it stayed in band for about 100 s, thousands of cycles, and matched filtering gains as the square root of cycles.
For the H0 story, first make sure the learner understands luminosity distance from a chirp (Chapter 9), then show the inclination degeneracy with the amplitude-ratio plot, then Figure 12.6.

Be explicit that numbers are as of mid-2021 and several printed equations have slips (T exponents, Eqs. 12.15, 12.18-12.19, the missing factor 2 in Eq. 12.29, Eq. 12.41, Eq. 12.47, the spin-down units in Exercise 12.9) and that Eq. 12.8 lacks the conventional factor 1/2; use corrected versions in derivations and say so if a learner quotes the book.

For advanced learners, extend with the continuous noise-weighted inner product (h|h) = 4 Re integral h*(f)h(f)/S_h(f) df and the standard antenna functions with polarization angle; for beginners, stay with the discrete toy model and the stories.

Suggested sequence for a 45-minute voice lesson: GW versus EM contrast (5 min), source zoo with scaling laws (10), matched filter toy model (10), false alarms and coincidence (8), null stream idea (5), GW170817 case study tying it together (7).
